How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2220 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.
  • In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens.
  • The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

We rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

In a recent development, the leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

Sources indicate that the first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

It has been revealed that the natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

Recent findings suggest that to see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

It has been revealed that think of a shipping manufacturer that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

Industry observers note that adapting a model's vocabulary is not a latest idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

They choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

Industry observers note that they work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

Sources indicate that first, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

In a recent development, second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping organization: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

Recent findings suggest that to find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

Sources indicate that third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents reveals up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

According to recent reports, A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

According to recent reports, to measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

In a recent development, the model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

Industry observers note that the lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

It has been revealed that to find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

Recent findings suggest that vocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

According to recent reports, vocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

It has been revealed that specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

Explore Dharma AI on Hugging Face to try our demos, download our open models, and see how specialized AI systems outperform general-purpose models in real enterprise applications.

Amazon RDS for Db2 now supports upcoming Canadian time zones

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (232 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that ​​Amazon RDS for Db2 now supports four newly introduced time zones, America/Vancouver, America/Edmonton, America/Inuvik, and America/Winnipeg, that reflect the updated local time rules for British Columbia, Alberta, the Northwest Territories, and Manitoba in Canada.
  • ​Data stored in UTC is unaffected, but values based on the instance's local time, such as CURRENT TIMESTAMP, CURRENT DATE, default timestamp columns, scheduled jobs, and business-day batch logic, can be affected.
  • Sources indicate that ​​You can select the new time zones when you create a new RDS for Db2 instance.

It has been revealed that ​​Amazon RDS for Db2 now supports four newly introduced time zones, America/Vancouver, America/Edmonton, America/Inuvik, and America/Winnipeg, that reflect the updated local time rules for British Columbia, Alberta, the Northwest Territories, and Manitoba in Canada. As of November 1, 2026, these provinces and territories observe permanent daylight saving time and no longer set their clocks back by an hour.​.

​Data stored in UTC is unaffected, but values based on the instance's local time, such as CURRENT TIMESTAMP, CURRENT DATE, default timestamp columns, scheduled jobs, and business-day batch logic, can be affected. With these newly introduced time zones, you can keep local time values accurate for workloads operating in these regions.

Sources indicate that ​​You can select the new time zones when you create a new RDS for Db2 instance. To change the time zone of an existing instance, contact AWS Support, as modifying the time zone of an existing instance is not supported through the AWS CLI, API, or SDK. If your instances serve workloads in these regions, we recommend reviewing them and updating your time zone configuration to avoid incorrect local times in your applications.​.

​The fresh time zones are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon RDS for Db2 is offered. To learn more and see the full list of supported time zones, visit the Amazon RDS for Db2 time zone documentation.​.

Ultimate guide for fixing your team’s API keys

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2087 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most Gemini prototypes start the same way.
  • The trouble starts later, when the prototype gets real users and the key comes along unchanged.
  • For example, imagine an account that normally spends $180 a month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Most Gemini prototypes start the same way. You grab an API key from Google AI Studio, then paste it into your coding agent to start building a prototype. That speed is the point, and shouldn’t be slowed down.

The trouble starts later, when the prototype gets real users and the key comes along unchanged. By then it usually isn't one key. Every developer has their own, often several, sitting in .env files, shell profiles and chat threads. The app has one more, baked into its config.

For example, imagine an account that normally spends $180 a month. One of those keys ends up in a public repo, a Slack channel or a mobile app bundle. Automated scrapers find it within minutes and use it to run large workloads. By the time the first billing alert arrives, the bill is in the tens of thousands. Under the shared responsibility model, the customer pays for usage made with their own valid credentials. For a seed-stage tech giant, that’s runway gone in a weekend.

Sources indicate that in our recent post, 10 questions every startup should answer before moving to production with their AI prototype, we covered the whole path from prototype to production. This post goes deeper on one part of it: getting off raw API keys entirely.

Here is what this guide covers:.

According to recent reports, authorize your people. Give everyone on the team one login with Application Default Credentials and use it to call Gemini, Claude and open models. Steps 1 and 2 take about five minutes.

It has been revealed that authorize your application. Run your app under its own service account with only the access it needs. Steps 3 and 4.

In a recent development, lock down what's left. Move the remaining keys into Secret Manager, then add spend caps, guardrails and monitoring. Step 5 and the closing sections.

The code for every step is in a companion repo with runnable samples and offline tests.

An AI Studio key is a bearer token. Whoever holds it can use it. It doesn't expire on its own. It isn't tied to a machine, a person or a workload. It has no spending limit unless you add one. When someone leaves the organization, nobody knows which keys to revoke.

Sources indicate that that is fine on your laptop while you are the only user. It stops being fine when any of these is true:.

Recent findings suggest that A key has left your laptop. It was shared in chat, committed to a repo or deployed to a server.

More than one person on the team needs to call the API.

You are spending more than a few hundred dollars a month, or you are about to onboard paying customers.

If one of those describes you, do the switch this week.

Before changing anything, find out where your keys are. The repo includes a small scanner that looks for strings shaped like Google API keys and for api_key= set to a literal value. It reports the file and line but never the key itself. It also exits with an error, so you can drop it into CI:.

Each person on the team runs one command:.

Industry observers note that A browser window opens, you sign in with your work account and gcloud stores a short-lived credential on your machine. Every Google Cloud SDK finds it automatically. There is no key to copy, paste or leak.

Then point your tools at the team project:.

It has been revealed that someone has to grant you access to the project first. Step four reveals how.

Industry observers note that that single credential works for every model in Model Garden, not only Gemini. You don't need upcoming accounts, new keys or separate invoices. Within each SDK, switching models means changing one string.

Gemini, with the Google Gen AI SDK. If your prototype builds the client with api_key=..., this is the only change:.

Recent findings suggest that enterprise=True sends the call to Gemini Platform instead of AI Studio. Older samples call the same flag vertexai=True, and current SDK versions accept both.

Claude, with Anthropic's SDK and the same login:.

Open models such as OpenAI's gpt-oss, with the OpenAI SDK pointed at Google Cloud:.

Partner models like Claude need a one-time Enable on their Model Garden card in each project. After that, everyone with access can call them.

It has been revealed that openAI's GPT-6 models arrived in Model Garden on October 21 in private preview for select enterprise customers. When they open up, the same login will work for them too.

Every call lands on one Google Cloud bill, which makes it easier to compare models on cost and quality.

In a recent development, your app needs the same thing your developers just got: an identity instead of a key. For a workload, that identity is a service account.

In a recent development, the good news is that the code from Step 2 doesn't change. On your laptop, ADC picks up your own login. On Cloud Run, GKE or Compute Engine, it picks up a short-lived token for the service account attached to the workload, refreshed automatically. So there is nothing in your codebase to leak. A token that escapes is short-lived, usually about an hour, and it only carries the permissions of one service account.

Create the service account and deploy with it:.

Industry observers note that keep people and production apart. Developers work in my-startup-dev under their own logins, and the app runs in my-startup-prod under its service account. A mistake in one doesn't spend the other's budget.

Removing keys solves the leak problem. The next question is what each identity is allowed to do. If a person or a service account holds the Editor or Owner role, a stolen login or token can still delete resources, change permissions or read data it never needed.

Calling models takes one role, roles/aiplatform.user. The grant looks the same for both kinds of identity.

For people, grant it to a Google group, not to individuals. Onboarding and offboarding then become a group membership change:.

For the app, grant it to the service account:.

It has been revealed that it takes about 30 seconds longer than granting Editor. If anything is compromised later, the attacker gets one narrow role instead of the whole project. When someone leaves, remove them from the group and their access ends everywhere at once.

It has been revealed that in the Cloud Console, the Grant access dialog has a Help me choose roles button. You describe the task in plain English and Gemini suggests predefined roles. By default the suggestions cover common tasks, which usually means a service's broad Admin, Editor or Viewer role. To get the narrow roles, say so:.

What is the narrowest access a service account needs to call Gemini models on Agent Platform?

Three more controls are worth knowing:.

In a recent development, if your project sits in an organization, the vertexai.allowedModels policy limits which models anyone can call. You list values such as publishers/google/models/gemini-4-hydrogen:predict, and everything else is blocked.

The repo includes a one-line audit that lists every service account holding Owner or Editor on a project. Run it now and again before each launch.

To stop upcoming keys from being created, enforce Org Policies denying CREATE on apikeys.googleapis.com/Key for API keys and iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation for service account keys.

In a recent development, some keys won't go away, like Stripe, Slack or your email provider. They belong in Secret Manager, not in .env files, chat threads or the repo. Access works the way it did in Step 4: grant read access on each secret to the identity that needs it.

Test keys go to the developer group:.

Anyone in the group can then fetch the key with their own login:.

Sources indicate that live keys stay in the production project, readable only by the app's service account. The app reads them at startup:.

It has been revealed that reading --data-file=- from standard input keeps the value out of your shell history. Every read is tied to a named person or service account, and rotating a key means adding one fresh version. Nothing is redeployed and no file is copied between laptops.

It has been revealed that then finish the job. Go to the AI Studio API keys page and delete every key, personal or shared, that ever left a laptop. A key you have moved away from is still live until you delete it.

Recent findings suggest that once your people and your app run on identities in a Google Cloud project, several protections become available that a bare key can't offer. You don't need all of them on day one. They are worth knowing about before your first launch.

According to recent reports, standard budget alerts send email while the bill keeps climbing. A spend cap budget, currently in Preview, does more. When estimated spend for one service in one project passes the amount you set, new requests to that service are paused until you lift the cap or the next month starts. Alerts go to billing admins and project owners at 50%, 80% and 100%.

You can create one in the console under Budgets & alerts by choosing Spend cap enforcement, or through the Budget API. The repo wraps the API call and has a dry-run flag so you can inspect the request first:.

Know the limits before relying on it. Each cap covers a single project and a single service. Agent Platform, the Gemini API, Cloud Run and Cloud Run functions are eligible today. Enforcement runs on estimated cost and is not instant. Any overage is billed as normal, so set the number below the amount you can actually afford to lose. A cap also pauses usage covered by commitments, and after you lift it the service can take up to an hour to recover.

In a recent development, set one cap on the dev project and another on prod. An experiment then can't drain the budget your customers depend on. For a second layer, lower your Agent Platform quotas to what you really need, so a bug or an agent stuck in a loop runs into a ceiling instead of your card limit.

Recent findings suggest that as soon as real consumers can type into your app, someone will try to make it ignore its instructions. Model Armor screens prompts and responses for prompt injection, jailbreak attempts, malicious URLs and sensitive data. You create a template once, check each prompt against it and only call the model when it comes back clean. The repo has both halves.

It has been revealed that if your product lets the model write and run code, for example to analyze a customer's spreadsheet, that code should not run inside your application process. With code execution, the model runs Python in a Google-managed sandbox and hands back the result:.

The generated code never sees your environment variables, your files or your database.

In a recent development, security Command Center surfaces threats and misconfigurations across the project, such as a service account suddenly calling an API it has never used or a workload contacting an unfamiliar host. Together with Cloud Audit Logs, which record who changed what and when, it also gives you the answers your first enterprise customer's security review will ask for. Because every call now comes from a named person or service account, those logs mean something.

Everyone runs gcloud auth application-default login.

Grant roles/aiplatform.user to one Google group, and enable the partner models you want.

Move shared test keys into Secret Manager, readable by the group.

Deploy with a service account that holds roles/aiplatform.user and nothing broader.

Move live third-party keys into Secret Manager, readable only by that service account.

Set a spend cap on each project below the amount you can afford to lose.

For both: Run the key scanner, then delete every AI Studio key at aistudio.google.com/apikey.

None of this slows down building. You keep the speed of the prototype and every model in Model Garden stays one string away. Nobody on the team has to guard a key again. The full code, with a sample for every step and bonus above, is in the companion repo.

Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3144 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Noted It Was Done.
  • We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome.
  • ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Noted It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

Figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

Each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

Industry observers note that then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+.

Sources indicate that so we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

According to recent reports, we call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

Industry observers note that we used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

Table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

Training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

Recent findings suggest that what does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but manufacturer policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

Industry observers note that figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

In a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

Recent findings suggest that thinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly new solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

In our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

And bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

According to recent reports, if you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 reveals which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

According to recent reports, the executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

Sources indicate that after training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

Table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

The headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

Average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

The observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

Overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

Sources indicate that figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

In a recent development, pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:.

Table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

Figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

The move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

The dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

It has been revealed that these results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

Figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

Sources indicate that selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

Industry observers note that every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

According to recent reports, training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

Industry observers note that for the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each update generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

In a recent development, zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

Recent findings suggest that that explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:.

No ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

According to recent reports, thinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

Why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++.

Recent findings suggest that A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

Sources indicate that so we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

Each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:.

success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½).

Recent findings suggest that figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

Recent findings suggest that we partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:.

Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

Sources indicate that figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO update.

According to recent reports, figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

In a recent development, nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

In a recent development, when an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

In a recent development, in the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

Two reward paths, one binary verdict.

Almost $1bn raised in FinTech deals in strong week for investment

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1982 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fintech

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Across the 17 deals reported on by FinTech Global this week, there was a total of $991m raised – showcasing a continuous strength in firms securing investment.
  • This was up on last week, where total of $602m was raised across 14 FinTech deals, a small increase on the previous week where $454.4m was raised across 12 deals.
  • Two of the top deals this week came from Bulgarian PayTech firm Payhawk and Model ML, a personal AI platform for financial and professional services.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Across the 17 deals reported on by FinTech Global this week, there was a total of $991m raised – showcasing a continuous strength in firms securing investment.

This was up on last week, where total of $602m was raised across 14 FinTech deals, a small increase on the previous week where $454.4m was raised across 12 deals.

Two of the top deals this week came from Bulgarian PayTech firm Payhawk and Model ML, a personal AI platform for financial and professional services.

Geographically, the US secured the most deals this week with 8 in total. Trailing in second was Canada with three, whilst Israel, Egypt, Spain, Georgia, the UK and Bulgaria pulled in one.

Market-wise, financial infrastructure firms made up the majority of this week’s deals with four. In joint second were WealthTech and CyberTech firms on three, PayTech, InsurTech and Blockchain firms secured two.

Sources indicate that this week, research from FinTech Global showcased findings of a powerful performance for Global FinTech in this year’s third quarter. The Global FinTech market attracted $27.5bn across 1,275 deals in Q3 2026. Funding climbed 35% from $20.3bn in Q3 2025 but fell 11% from $30.9bn in Q2 2026.

Deal volume fell 2% from 1,306 transactions in Q3 2025 and rose 5% from 1,220 in Q2 2026.

Payhawk raises $280m to build AI-era Finance OS.

Payhawk, the Sofia-founded spend management and finance platform, has closed a $280m Series C round led by Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives. The deal values the tech giant at $2bn.

The raise takes Payhawk’s total funding past $515m. Every existing backer returned for the round, among them QED, Greenoaks, Lightspeed, Hedosophia and Bek Ventures.

They were joined by first-time investors Galdana Ventures, Cogito Capital, Inveready and Invus, as well as European founders Tomas Okmanas and Didac Lee.

Model ML bags $250m to give every banker an AI agent.

Model ML, a London-based personal AI platform for financial and professional services, has secured $250m in a Series B round that values the company at $1.5bn.

General Atlantic and QED Investors co-led the investment. Evolution Equity Partners, Airtree, Forestay Capital, Y Combinator, FT Partners, Latitude, Inception Fund and 13Books Capital also took part. The deal lifts the total capital raised by Model ML to $350m.

It has been revealed that the raise comes after a period of rapid expansion. Over the third quarter of 2026, annual recurring revenue at the firm increased twelvefold compared with the same period a year earlier, while daily active consumers rose 26-fold.

Blue J lands $176m to put AI agents on tax desks.

Blue J, a tax research and advisory platform, has secured $176m in a Series E round that values the business at above $700m, as it moves beyond answering tax questions to handing the actual workload over to AI agents.

JMI Equity, a growth equity investor, led the raise. Existing backers Oak HC/FT and Sapphire Ventures returned for the round, joined by Intrepid Growth Partners. The valuation also exceeds C$1bn. As part of the deal, JMI Equity principal Jack Duane will take a seat on the Blue J board.

The tech giant plans to put the capital behind Workflows, its agentic AI product for tax practitioners, and to push further into the United Kingdom and other international markets.

Corma hits $1bn valuation with $125m Series A.

Corma, an AI research lab building foundation models for defensive cybersecurity, has secured $125m in Series A funding at a $1bn valuation, only three months after revealing its seed round.

NEA led the investment, with participation from returning backers Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures and Coatue. The latest raise takes the manufacturer’s total funding to $185m.

Corma’s $60m seed round, led by Sequoia, was revealed in August.

TBC Georgia secures $51m as ADB and IFC back trade finance.

TBC Georgia, a leading Georgian financial institution and member of the London-listed TBC Bank Group, has raised $51m from international commercial banks to widen the availability of trade finance for businesses across Georgia.

The capital comes with guarantee backing from the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and the International Finance Corporation (IFC).

In a recent development, it is channelled through two established schemes: the ADB’s Trade and Supply Chain Finance Program and the IFC’s Global Trade Finance Program. Because both institutions stand behind the facility, commercial lenders can extend capital to the Georgian market with added assurance.

Codex lands $30m Series A to scale stablecoin FX.

Codex, a platform that provides foreign exchange infrastructure for stablecoins and fiat currencies, has secured $30m in Series A funding to expand its cross-border payments business.

Recent findings suggest that pantera headed the investment, which also drew backing from Dragonfly, Coinbase Ventures, Tenet, Reciprocal, Fin Capital, LeadBlock and additional investors. The deal puts the company’s post-money valuation at $130m.

Both Dragonfly and Coinbase Ventures have backed Codex before, having taken part in its seed round.

Arva AI lands $20m Series A for AI banking agents.

Arva AI, a organization that deploys AI agents to make critical banking decisions, has secured $20m in Series A funding as it looks to push its accuracy-focused technology deeper into the bank back office.

Industry observers note that according to the company, most back-office decisions at banks are still made manually, but this has begun to shift. Over the past year, Arva’s customers started entrusting important decisions to its agents, with staff setting policies and monitoring outcomes.

During that period the firm rolled out its technology at scale with banks and FinTechs, among them a top-10 US bank, a payments institution listed on the S&P 500 and the global FinTech Wise.

StepSecurity bags $20m as supply chain attacks escalate.

Elephant led the round, and existing backers Runtime Ventures, Inner Loop Capital and SaaS Ventures also took part. Together with a $3m seed round raised earlier, the deal lifts StepSecurity’s total funding to $23m.

The tech giant looks to use the money to speed up development and wider rollout of its platform, which is designed to stop malicious packages at every checkpoint of the agentic software pipeline.

Vero Security raises $11m as AI security jobs go unstaffed.

Vero Security, a start-up developing a platform for AI Security Engineering, has closed an $11m seed round as large enterprises struggle to staff a responsibility that most still treat as a side duty.

TLV Partners led the investment, joined by GTM Capital, Maple Capital and a group of angel backers. Vero was established in 2025 and has already signed several Fortune 500 businesses as customers.

Alongside the raise, it is introducing AISecurityEngineering.org, an open community and knowledge hub offering practical field guides, workshops and the ASE credential track for practitioners shaping this fresh specialism.

Roadzen raises $10m for India arm at $300m valuation.

Roadzen, which applies AI to insurance and mobility, has secured roughly $10m (₹94 crore) for its Indian subsidiary, Roadzen AI Limited, which is now valued at about $300m post-money on a stand-alone basis.

The round is being raised entirely as common equity. It carries no warrants or preferred rights, and the newly introduced shares rank equally with those held by the existing shareholder, Roadzen.

Sources indicate that because the capital goes into the subsidiary, shareholders in the Nasdaq-listed parent will not be diluted. Family offices and capital markets investors anchored the deal. Several of them had backed the organization’s earlier India subsidiary round and raised their commitments this time.

Valeria bags €5.5m seed to scale AI payroll engine.

Valeria, a Barcelona-headquartered payroll and workforce management platform built on artificial intelligence, has secured €5.5m in seed funding to expand its technology for businesses that see frequent staff changes.

The round was led by BlackFin, with returning backers VentureFriends and Fortino also participating. GoHub Ventures came on board as a upcoming investor in the tech giant.

The seed raise follows a €1.7m pre-seed round completed in February 2026, meaning Valeria has secured over €7m in total during 2026.

WealthTech finny raises Rs 5.3 Cr angel round.

finny, a WealthTech start-up offering personalised financial advice, has reportedly secured Rs 5.3 Cr (around $560,000) through an angel round, according to a report from BW Disrupt.

According to recent reports, A group of high-profile backers joined the round. Among them were Ramanathan RV, who founded both Hyperface and Juspay, and Anil Goel, who serves as Global CTO at Nielsen. Uday Sodhi, previously an executive at Sony Pictures, also took part, as did Aditya Pittie, MD and CEO of Pittie Group. Angel syndicate Zorvian LLP was among the other participants.

It has been revealed that the manufacturer intends to split the latest money across three priorities. A portion will go towards R&D, with an emphasis on building out its AI-driven products.

Pretxt raises $5m to keep AI agents within the rules.

Pretxt, a newly rolled out enterprise AI organization focused on runtime oversight of AI agents, has stepped out of stealth mode with $5m in seed capital to build out a technology category it calls AI Supervision.

Sources indicate that deciens Capital, Howdy Partners, Service Provider Capital and NSV Wolf Capital backed the round. Pretxt intends to use the capital to bring its supervision layer to enterprises that want AI agents to handle higher-stakes work without drifting from approved procedures.

In a recent development, AI agents no longer simply produce text. They now speak with customers, connect to other systems, handle transactions and run business processes. According to Pretxt, these agents do not always behave as instructed.

Verlo raises $4.5m to cut admin work for wealth firms.

Verlo, a provider of an AI operating system built for wealth management firms, has secured $4.5m CAD in seed funding to help Registered Investment Advisors (RIAs) cut back on time-consuming administrative tasks.

Staircase Ventures led the investment, while Pelorus VC came back to back the company again. They were joined by several angel investors, among them founders and senior executives from Verafin, the Newfoundland financial crime software business that Nasdaq bought in 2020 for $2.7bn.

Global Kiwi Labs raises $4m for TheHUB.

Global Kiwi Labs, the developer behind digital asset colocation network TheHUB, has closed a $4m seed round as it looks to bring the equal-access trading architecture used by major traditional exchanges to digital asset markets.

Industry observers note that valor Capital Group led the round. Adderall Capital, Keyrock and Staking Facilities also invested, alongside a small number of angel backers.

TheHUB’s first site, which is located within the Equinix TY15 data centre in Tokyo and is now live and bringing on exchanges, trading firms and validators. The manufacturer will also use the money to add engineers to its team and move into further regions.

Connect Money raises $3.5m to enter Saudi Arabia and Morocco.

Connect Money, an Egypt-based FinTech offering embedded finance and white-label card services, has secured $3.5m in a pre-Series A round as it gears up to take its platform into Saudi Arabia and Morocco.

The round was led by returning backers Mohamed Farouk, Algebra Ventures and DisrupTech Ventures, according to a report from Wamda.

Industry observers note that the deal blends newly introduced funding with the sale of secondary shares, giving a number of the startup’s early backers a partial exit. Connect Money has not revealed what portion of the $3.5m is new capital.

Eight by Zero lands $3m seed to fix insurance integration.

Eight by Zero, a Montréal-based InsurTech offering a universal interoperability platform for the insurance sector, has secured $3m in seed funding to expand its connectivity technology across more lines of coverage.

The round was led by Diagram, with Canada Life joining as a strategic investor.

Alongside the raise, the company, also known as 8/0, has named Munich Re Life US, part of the Munich Re Group, as its reinsurance partner. The two businesses are collaborating to tackle the difficulties group and disability insurance clients face in keeping employee data connected.

​​​Amazon RDS for Db2 now supports renaming databases​

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (166 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that ​​Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for Db2 now supports renaming databases in place.
  • In a recent development, ​​Database rename simplifies workflows such as replacing a database with a restored copy.
  • Industry observers note that ​​Database rename is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon RDS for Db2 is offered.

Recent findings suggest that ​​Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for Db2 now supports renaming databases in place. You can rename a database on your DB instance by calling the upcoming rdsadmin.rename_database stored procedure. Previously, renaming a database required you to back it up and restore it under a new name. With rename, the database keeps its data in place, so it's faster than backing up and restoring the database.​.

In a recent development, ​​Database rename simplifies workflows such as replacing a database with a restored copy. For example, after you restore a copy of a database from a backup, you can rename the original database, and then give its name to the restored copy, without changing your application connection strings. Database rename runs as a background task that you can monitor with rdsadmin.get_task_status.​.

Industry observers note that ​​Database rename is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon RDS for Db2 is offered. To get started, see the Amazon RDS User Guide.​​.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package).
  • The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub.
  • The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

Recent findings suggest that to look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We initiative to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

Recent findings suggest that select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:.

No need for torchrun: the script releases its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

It has been revealed that A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:.

Sources indicate that each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel strategy use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

Recent findings suggest that at the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

Everything the Space reveals comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

Industry observers note that each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:.

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime instances now support Amazon EC2 G7 instances, powered by NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs. Runtime instances run your agents on Amazon EC2 instances while AgentCore handles provisioning, patching, scaling, and lifecycle management. G7 instances give agents that do 3D rendering or model inference another GPU option, alongside families such as G6e and G7e.

Industry observers note that to use G7, add G7 instance types, from g7.2xlarge to g7.48xlarge, to the allowed instance types of your capacity provider. AgentCore installs the NVIDIA drivers on the instance, so standard container images run GPU workloads without bundling drivers. For example, an agent can render 3D scenes or run a vision model on its own GPU, in sessions of up to 14 days.

G7 instances on runtime instances are available in select AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (London), Europe (Stockholm), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), and Asia Pacific (Sydney). You are charged for managing the provisioned compute, in addition to your Amazon EC2 costs.

Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1292 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • LFM3 is our latest generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence.
  • LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.
  • LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LFM3 is our latest generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.

LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:.

According to recent reports, the payoff demonstrates at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

In a recent development, every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two fresh in-house encoders:.

Recent findings suggest that each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

Industry observers note that reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:.

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

In a recent development, reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:.

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

In a recent development, reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:.

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:.

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:.

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

Sources indicate that reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:.

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:.

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

Recent findings suggest that reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:.

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:.

For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

It has been revealed that LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

Recent findings suggest that we adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video.

All LFM3 models are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:.

We can't wait to see what you build.

If you use this work, please cite the release blog:.

💡 Key Takeaways

Recent findings suggest that AWS CloudFormation now supports up to 300,000 stacks in each AWS account and Region by default (previously 2,000), which enables you to add stacks as your workloads grow without requesting a quota increase. CloudFormation manages related AWS resources as a stack that you create, enhancement, and delete as one unit. Teams that deploy a separate stack for each customer, environment, or developer can now scale those patterns within a single account.

It has been revealed that A higher default quota allows you to keep growing workloads in the accounts where they already run. Previously, accounts that needed more than 2,000 stacks in a Region requested a quota increase through Service Quotas. Now, the default quota covers these workloads without a request. For example, a software provider that deploys one stack for each customer can grow from 2,000 to 300,000 customer stacks in one account and Region. Existing stacks work without changes.

It has been revealed that the higher quota applies to stacks you create in the CloudFormation console or with the AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, AWS CDK, or AWS SAM. To view your stacks per account quota, open the Service Quotas console. For more information, see CloudFormation quotas in the AWS CloudFormation User Guide. The increased quota is available at no additional charge in all AWS Regions where AWS CloudFormation is supported. For Region availability, see the AWS Region table.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AWS Data Exports for Cost and Usage Report (CUR) 2.0 now includes standardized cost and rate columns that represent cost consistently across AWS purchase options, including On Demand, Savings Aims, Reserved Instances, EC2 Spot, and EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML.
  • Industry observers note that previously, calculating savings required combining CUR with Savings Aims rates and public price lists, and amortized cost used different columns for each pricing model.
  • It has been revealed that standardized cost and rate columns are available at no additional charge in all AWS Regions except the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and the China Regions.

AWS Data Exports for Cost and Usage Report (CUR) 2.0 now includes standardized cost and rate columns that represent cost consistently across AWS purchase options, including On Demand, Savings Aims, Reserved Instances, EC2 Spot, and EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML. These 14 columns are added when you enable Include Standardized cost and rate columns while setting up a fresh CUR 2.0 export or editing an existing CUR 2.0 and these columns have the prefix cost_analytics_. With these new columns, you can quantify the savings you realize from commitments, discounts, and tiered pricing, and analyze amortized cost the same way for every pricing model with multiple payment options, directly in CUR 2.0.

Industry observers note that previously, calculating savings required combining CUR with Savings Aims rates and public price lists, and amortized cost used different columns for each pricing model. Now each line item carries billed, effective, list, contracted, public on-demand cost, the public equivalent of billed and effective cost before discounts, and a rate for each, so you can measure savings and amortized cost without building your own calculations. To add the columns, select Include standardized cost and rate columns when you create or edit a CUR 2.0 export. In Cost Explorer, choose the latest cost types under Advanced options to see the same costs.

It has been revealed that standardized cost and rate columns are available at no additional charge in all AWS Regions except the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and the China Regions. To learn more, see the CUR 2.0 data dictionary and the user guide for Cost Explorer.
