Industry News: What a billion-dollar deal claims about the US battery market

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (670 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.
  • In a recent development, sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries.
  • Industry observers note that this arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.

In a recent development, sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries. It’s a deal that Sila notes could be worth more than $1 billion over time.

Industry observers note that this arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately. A major part of the financial backing for this factory’s production is a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department. While batteries can be a major tool to help drive the energy transition and cut emissions, right now much of the industry is more focused on geopolitics.

It has been revealed that founded in 2011, Sila makes silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries. The major selling point here is the potential to improve energy density—Sila’s anode weighs a fifth as much as the graphite used in anodes today and cuts the volume in half, according to the company. So using this newly introduced material enables batteries to pack more energy into the same weight and volume, allowing longer range for EVs, for example. The material can also deliver more power and recharge faster, compared with conventional chemistry.

We’ve been following Sila (and its competitors) for years. My colleague James Temple covered the organization when its battery first appeared in Whoop fitness wearables in 2021.

Sources indicate that things have gotten a lot bigger since then. In 2022, Sila unveiled plans for a factory in Moses Lake, Washington, and received $100 million from the US Department of Energy, part of a multibillion-dollar round of grants under the Biden administration to support the US battery supply chain.

The organization opened its factory in September 2025, and it’s already operating. But the deal with Panasonic will help it scale to at least 10 times more production than current levels, states Gene Berdichevsky, the company’s cofounder and CEO.

Panasonic has committed to buying tens of thousands of tons of material, Berdichevsky states, though Sila isn’t sharing specific numbers on the total commitment or the price Panasonic is paying.

Recent findings suggest that this agreement is Sila’s first mass-market deal and a big one for the United States’ next-generation battery market, which has largely been on the ropes over the past few years. Two billion-dollar battery companies, 24M and ESS Tech, have declared bankruptcy and shut down just in the last year.

It has been revealed that the glimmer of hope here is tied up with something I’ve been noticing about this industry: the shifting politics. While batteries used to be firmly considered a climate technology, we’ve seen a lot of companies move away from messaging around the clean energy transition and lean into geopolitics.

China dominates the battery world and particularly the battery anode market, controlling over 90% of graphite production today. For years, the US has been trying to curb reliance on Chinese batteries, battery materials, and other materials used in crucial technologies, like rare earth metals. But the Trump administration has ramped things up, and earlier this year the US Defense Department committed a $1.4 billion loan to Sila aimed at helping the US face a “significant technology sovereignty challenge,” as a press release put it.

Industry observers note that sila’s announcement of the Panasonic deal does mention EVs—but not climate, emissions or the energy transition. Rather, it’s all about American industrialization. (And, of course, a mention that a North American battery supply chain can also help power the AI market.).

I asked Berdichevsky about this shift and whether the firm holds decarbonization as a priority.

It has been revealed that “I think the politics of it has shifted around us much more than our motivations have shifted,” he remarked. “It’s really the energy efficiency that motivates engineers like myself and technologists at our organization. And I still think that that’s still at the heart of it.”.

Latest Update: Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A New Frontier and Use Cases

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads.
  • Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory.
  • Sources indicate that the challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs.

Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next.

Sources indicate that the challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome.

It has been revealed that IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action.

It has been revealed that foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to newly introduced series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic.

Figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them.

It has been revealed that now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy (documentation). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.(documentation). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs.

It has been revealed that the models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made.

See how time series and real-time context come together to create value:.

Recent findings suggest that businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that enhancement at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening.

Industry observers note that A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state.

It has been revealed that figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere.

According to recent reports, time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate.

Recent findings suggest that figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them.

This approach can help teams in four ways:.

-Scale model development. A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one.

-Refresh predictions as data changes. Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration.

According to recent reports, -Put signals closer to decisions. Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment.

It has been revealed that -Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment.

Figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent.

The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic.

An ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a new cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result.

To get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range.

When the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails.

The outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills.

Figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment.

A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus.

AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each new reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store.

It has been revealed that when sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes.

Figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged.

It has been revealed that A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock.

Industry observers note that with AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as upcoming sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point.

When stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand.

Figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk.

Sources indicate that fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends.

In a recent development, A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules.

Industry observers note that the bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review.

Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow.

It has been revealed that an execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average.

In a recent development, on each one-minute bar, PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume for the next 30 minutes, with a P10–P90 range. The execution algorithm uses that forecast to pace the order within the participation limit set by the desk.

If a news event changes market activity, the algorithm can pause and replan. If trading is quieter than expected, it can reduce the size of each slice and signal that the order may take longer to complete. Each forecast and the resulting execution decisions can be retained in the audit trail.

Figure 9. Volume forecast informs the proposed execution schedule for a 100,000-share order.

A reliability engineer investigating an unusual sensor pattern may want to know whether similar behavior appeared elsewhere in the plant.

It has been revealed that TSPulse can produce representations of time-series windows that support similarity search. In a separately built application, those representations could be indexed and used to retrieve historical patterns across equipment. An engineer could search for shapes such as a spike and recovery, a gradual rise, or a step change, then inspect the associated maintenance records and operating conditions.

According to recent reports, this application requires an embedding pipeline, an index, and access to the relevant context. Similarity can help narrow an investigation; it does not establish a root cause by itself.

Sources indicate that figure 10. Time-series embeddings can support a search for similar patterns across equipment and other signals.

The same models and building blocks can support different workflows across industries:.

Sources indicate that figure 11. The plant twin, from sensor to setpoint. A fresh cream lot pulls overrun off target. The forecast reads the line, the agent proposes a new draw temperature and air flow, the operator approves, and the tubs are back in spec. Simulated data.

Figure 12. The store twin, a store and its supply chain. A promo is coming for oat milk. The forecast prices in the promo and sets the reorder point, the agent raises a purchase order, the planner approves, and the shelf is full on promo day. Simulated data.

In a recent development, banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. Every card and every symbol is scored against its own expected pattern, event by event. Fraud and security holds the odd swipe before authorization, anomaly detection spots the unusual flow, and trading paces each order with the forecast volume.

Airlines: hub operations, fleet and network. Operations control wants to see a disruption coming while there is still time to act. Engine, gate and network streams are forecast and checked in real time. Anomaly detection catches the engine reading that drifts, production optimization rebalances gates and crews, and supply chain planning puts the spare part where the aircraft will be.

In every industry, the Streamhouse does the same work: Flink runs the Granite models to forecast, detect and optimize, Streaming Agents act on the live context, and people approve the exceptions.

Breaking: A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1031 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative newly introduced possibilities in biomedical engineering.
  • The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.
  • In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative newly introduced possibilities in biomedical engineering.

The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.

In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System.

“Our group is the only one in the world to have maintained a human liver under fully normothermic, physiological conditions for seven weeks,” he states.

Normothermic means body temperature, or about 37 °C. The previous record for keeping an internal organ alive outside the body was set in Switzerland several years ago. That organ—also a liver—lasted around two weeks.

Sources indicate that most organs destined for transplant survive only a few hours in special ice buckets and need to be raced to their destination. Over the last decade, however, surgeons have been switching to perfusion systems, which pump warm or cold fluids into an organ. This can double the time it can be held before it must be transplanted.

Pulitano indicates the key to breaking the record was to automate the systems used to keep the organ thriving. During a meeting in Switzerland earlier this year, the Sydney team described perfusing 55 human livers, one after the other. Some were connected to a system that needed to be adjusted manually, but for those placed on the automated system—which produced the seven-week survivor—the average survival time tripled, to about four weeks.

Perfusion has already enabled doctors to restart hearts from dead people and keep them beating outside the body. Paulo Martins, a transplant doctor at the University of Oklahoma, claims about half the kidneys he transplants are now perfused, even though the process can add $100,000 to the cost of a transplant.

While the research awaits formal publication, the eventual goal is what Pulitano and colleagues call “time-unlimited liver preservation.”.

In a recent development, scientists have already discovered possible medical benefits to keeping organs on life support longer than usual. One, they say, is that perfused organs apparently start to repair themselves and become stronger after a day or so. That’s what led a Swiss team, in 2022, to transplant a damaged liver that had been kept on perfusion for three days—the longest time any internal organ had remained outside the body before a successful transplant, indicates Waldemar Hoffmann, the CEO and cofounder of Apersys, a startup formed to commercialize the technology.

Pulitano says his own startup, Aeternum Life Technologies, will be helping with a planned trial in Sydney to transplant low-quality livers kept on perfusion for four days.

What’s less clear, states Hoffmann, is whether any transplant surgeon would ever want, or need, to use an organ kept alive for nearly two months. He says people in the field believe Pulitano’s record is real, but they don’t know how healthy the organ was at the end or even what so much extra time is likely to achieve. “The key question is what the purpose for a seven-week perfusion would be,” he says.

Industry observers note that yet that’s where things could start to get interesting, says Martins, the Oklahoma surgeon. Long-term life support could enable far-out concepts like artificial wombs, new types of organ manufacturing, and the chance to experiment directly on human organs outside the body for extended periods.

Recent findings suggest that for his part, Pulitano says long-term machine perfusion could help grow newly introduced organs. In living donations, surgeons commonly take half of a person’s liver to give someone else. After about two months, both parts will have grown back almost to their full volume. Pulitano says he’s tried dividing a liver and then attaching the sections to the machine. If that works, he says, it could be a way to multiply one donor liver into several full-size organs.

“It’s notable to have people thinking outside the box and pushing the limits and creating possibilities for things that, right now, sometimes we don’t even have a need for but are going to be needed in the future,” states Martins. “That’s how science moves.”.

He’s not the only one who thinks so. For instance, a US manufacturer, Bexorg, has been reanimating human brains using perfusion pumps. The idea is to study what effects experimental drugs have on them. That company perfuses brains for about a day but has remarked it wants to extend the time to two weeks.

Similar experiments can be done on livers, says Pulitano, who has already tried adding gene therapies to the organs. “It gives us a living human organ model for translational research that no animal system can match, because the biology, the immunology, and the drug responses are human from the outset,” he says.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, in Silicon Valley, patents filed by Altos Labs, a billionaire-backed longevity startup, describe attempts to introduce reprogramming genes into animal livers maintained outside the body. Eventually, Altos scientists have speculated, they might temporarily disconnect a failing organ while it’s still in a person’s body, connecting it to a perfusion machine in order to douse it with ultra-powerful genetic treatments without risking the rest of the body.

According to recent reports, doctors probing the limits of organ life support have now formed two new scientific societies to explore the concept. One, founded by Martins and called the International Society for Organ Preservation and Perfusion Therapy, will hold its inaugural meeting this year in Italy. The other, based in China, was rolled out in August to advance what doctors at the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University have termed “organ medicine”: research at the level of whole organs kept alive by “bionic maintenance.”.

“What is exploding is the idea of this technology that clearly goes beyond simply organ preservation,” indicates Pulitano. “Basically, that’s a concept that’s entirely latest.”.

Breaking: AWS Lambda now supports a batch size of up to 10,000 messages for Amazon SQS FIFO queues

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (285 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, AWS Lambda now supports a batch size of up to 10,000 messages for Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue event source mappings (ESMs) in provisioned mode, up from 10 messages previously.
  • Customers use SQS FIFO queues with Lambda to build event-driven applications that need strict message ordering and deduplication.
  • This feature is available for SQS FIFO ESMs in provisioned mode in all AWS commercial Regions.

According to recent reports, AWS Lambda now supports a batch size of up to 10,000 messages for Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue event source mappings (ESMs) in provisioned mode, up from 10 messages previously. With larger batches, you can process high-volume, ordered workloads such as financial transactions, order processing, and inventory updates with fewer invocations and higher throughput. Lambda continues to preserve message ordering within each message group.

Customers use SQS FIFO queues with Lambda to build event-driven applications that need strict message ordering and deduplication. With provisioned mode for SQS ESMs, you can use throughput controls to set a minimum and maximum number of event pollers to meet strict performance requirements. Previously, provisioned mode customers who needed higher throughput for SQS FIFO queues were limited by the maximum batch size of 10 messages. This required them to scale out invocations or add custom buffering logic, which added operational overhead and cost. With this launch, you can set a batch size of up to 10,000 messages and a batching window of up to 300 seconds for FIFO queues, so you can process large volumes of ordered messages in fewer invocations without re-architecting your applications.

This feature is available for SQS FIFO ESMs in provisioned mode in all AWS commercial Regions. You can configure the batch size and the batching window when you create new ESMs or update existing ESMs by using the Lambda console, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, AWS CloudFormation, AWS CDK, or AWS SAM. You can also use coding assistants such as Kiro, Claude Code, or Codex with the Agent Toolkit for AWS. To learn more, visit the AWS Lambda Developer Guide and the AWS Lambda pricing.

#22131. Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1394 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1394 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.
  • It has been revealed that A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models.
  • Recent findings suggest that GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.

It has been revealed that A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.

Recent findings suggest that GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That proposal is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.

Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It indicates nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.

The short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.

For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:.

Industry observers note that here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.

In a recent development, this is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.

According to recent reports, these overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.

We treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.

Two design choices shaped the work:.

We compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.

Distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

All numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.

No single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.

Industry observers note that A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That says nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It highlights how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

According to recent reports, linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.

Gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.

Industry observers note that catBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.

Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).

It has been revealed that feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.

In a recent development, one caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.

Sources indicate that looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:.

Up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.

Industry observers note that out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.

More data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can plan around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

Recent findings suggest that what does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.

Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.

The full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.

Designing the most performant chips for AI workloads sits at the heart of accelerating technological progress.

According to recent reports, first, chip design is slow. It takes 12-24 months at mature nodes and 18-36 months at the leading edge for 5nm or 3nm.

Industry observers note that second, chip design is prohibitively expensive. It costs on average $200-250 million for 7nm, $450-500 million for 5nm, and $600-650 million for 3nm. Roughly 50-70% of that is human labor. Another 5-15% is Electronic Design Automation tooling spend in a market long dominated by Cadence and Synopsys, where each generates $5-6 billion in annual revenue and are worth approximately $90-100 billion in market cap.

Sources indicate that alphaChip caught my eye for these exact reasons. It gave us a peek at AIâs potential to transform the entire chip design process, showing we can cut the floorplanning step in physical design from months to hours.

What if we could extrapolate this and build AI to automate the entire flow, from architecture design to RTL to verification, all the way through physical design?

What if chip design took days, not two to three years? Every day is massively costly; some reports from August 2024 indicated that a multi-month Blackwell delay could result in more than $10 billion in lost revenue for 2025 alone. More importantly, imagine the revenue potential unlocked when new generations of chips are designed faster and shipped earlier.

What if each design didnât cost hundreds of millions of dollars? What if chip companies didnât need to operate large human teams on top of clunky EDA tooling?

And most exciting: what if we unlocked novel chip designs we might never have explored?

AlphaChip revealed an crucial human bias: in chip design, we tend to think in Manhattan grid-like structures. AlphaChipâs designs were different, more organic in shape, more like forms inspired by nature. So different, in fact, that humans wanted to reject them at first â¦ Yet AlphaChip went on to shape four generations of the TPU.

Recent findings suggest that we at Sequoia are so excited to partner with co-founders Anna Goldie and Azalia Mirhoseini, leading their very first round from the formation of Ricursive Intelligence. They pioneered AI for chip design by creating and leading the AlphaChip effort and are at the epicenter of this emerging AI for chip design ecosystem. They are visionaries with incredible clarity of thought, intensely ambitious, humble yet exceptionally accomplished, and real talent magnets who move, and inspire others to move, with urgency and velocity.

Anna and Azalia founded Ricursive Intelligence to build the frontier AI lab defining this category. In just the first weeks since firm formation, they have assembled a team with the highest talent density you can imagine in the field.

Their core belief: chip design is the compute bottleneck, and progress in AI, hardware and infrastructure is capped by the speed and efficiency of silicon creation.

In their words: âIf we get this right, itâs not just faster chip design cycles; itâs a fundamental expansion of whatâs possible in hardware. Once chip design becomes fast and accessible, everyone will be able to customize. The automation here will unlock a flood of newly introduced hardware innovation.â.

Anna and Azaliaâs vision for Ricursive is to define a new movement, from âfablessâ to âdesignless.â Fabless, meaning a organization designing chips without owning expensive fabs, outsourcing production to foundries. Designless, meaning outsourcing not only manufacturing but the entire chip design process, taking an idea and converting it into a manufacturable design.

We envision a world where Ricursive helps any organization design chips for its own workloads faster, more efficiently and more creatively than is possible today. In doing so, Ricursive can help revolutionize the most valuable resource in our era: compute. We could not be more excited to help build a true generational company in the making.

  • Data quality monitoring for catalogs and databases in AWS Glue Data Catalog is available in all AWS Commercial, AWS GovCloud (US), and AWS China regions.
  • It has been revealed that to get started, create a data quality configuration by using the AWS CLI, API, or SDKs, which support built-in profiling and custom DQDL rulesets at the catalog, database, or table level.

It has been revealed that you can use built-in profiling options that AWS Glue provides for common baseline statistics or provide your own Data Quality Definition Language (DQDL) ruleset with analyzers, rules, or both to hold every table in a database to the same quality standards. You have the flexibility to run evaluations once when you create the configuration or set up triggers, so evaluations run on a schedule or whenever table metadata changes, including every Apache Iceberg commit. After three runs on a table, AWS Glue Data Quality flags anomalous statistics that drift outside expected bounds, surfacing changes that no rule covers. Results are accessible through the existing AWS Glue Data Quality APIs, or you can opt-in to write them to Apache Iceberg tables in the AWS Glue Data Catalog or to Amazon S3.

Data quality monitoring for catalogs and databases in AWS Glue Data Catalog is available in all AWS Commercial, AWS GovCloud (US), and AWS China regions.

It has been revealed that to get started, create a data quality configuration by using the AWS CLI, API, or SDKs, which support built-in profiling and custom DQDL rulesets at the catalog, database, or table level. In Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, you can turn on profiling for a catalog or database from the catalog page. To learn more, visit the AWS Glue Data Quality documentation and the Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio documentation.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles.
  • In a recent development, the model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window.
  • We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:.

In a recent development, the model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.

We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.

After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:.

In a recent development, the model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.

DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.

Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.

Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.

Recent findings suggest that we built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.

We selected tasks using three criteria:.

RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

It has been revealed that stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

Industry observers note that every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.

Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.

Our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.

The service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.

Cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.

Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.

We’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.

According to recent reports, we thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.

AWS Lambda now provides cost optimization recommendations for Event Functions

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (306 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AWS Lambda now provides cost optimization recommendations for Event Functions in AWS Trusted Advisor.
  • LMI lets you run Lambda functions on Amazon EC2 instances while maintaining the operational simplicity of Lambda.
  • According to recent reports, these recommendations are available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N.

AWS Lambda now provides cost optimization recommendations for Event Functions in AWS Trusted Advisor. These recommendations identify on-demand functions where moving to Lambda Managed Instances (LMI) is estimated to reduce costs, and provide configuration guidance for running on LMI. With these recommendations, you can lower your Lambda costs by focusing your efforts on the functions with the greatest estimated savings.

LMI lets you run Lambda functions on Amazon EC2 instances while maintaining the operational simplicity of Lambda. With LMI, you can access specialized compute configurations and drive cost efficiency through EC2 pricing options such as Savings Prepares and Reserved Instances, without managing infrastructure. Previously, to determine whether a function was a good fit for LMI, you had to analyze its invocation patterns, estimate LMI costs, and select the right instance type and memory-to-vCPU ratio yourself. This manual process added overhead and delayed savings. With this launch, Lambda automatically analyzes the invocation patterns, duration, and resource utilization of your high-volume Event Functions and recommends those where LMI is estimated to reduce costs. Estimates are based on a simulation of each function's invocation patterns, using public Lambda pricing and Amazon EC2 On-Demand pricing. Each recommendation includes the function ARN, the recommended EC2 instance type and memory-to-vCPU ratio, the estimated current cost, the estimated LMI cost, and the estimated savings. You can use the recommended configuration to run a function on LMI without sizing it yourself and realize cost savings sooner.

According to recent reports, these recommendations are available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Europe (Ireland), and Europe (Milan). Customers with eligible AWS Support aims can access them in the Trusted Advisor console alongside other cost optimization checks. To learn more, visit the AWS Lambda Developer Guide, the AWS Trusted Advisor User Guide, and the AWS Lambda pricing.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1290 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.
  • In a recent development, the report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared—and widely misinterpreted, owing to the complexity of the measures it used.
  • In a recent development, the updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.

In a recent development, the report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared—and widely misinterpreted, owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot demonstrated that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled.

In a recent development, the updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work.

In a recent development, it’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a latest research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development.

And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement.

METR researchers have worked to make sure their latest suite of tasks includes some of the fuzzier, judgment-laden ones that could be most relevant to AI research and development. In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results. Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research.

In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments. This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about how relevant the task is for automation of AI R&D. On this task, too, models fell short of human performance.

Though it’s difficult to score these new tasks—and even harder to determine what the scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into its work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” states Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.”.

Recent findings suggest that kapoor says he wasn’t surprised to see that models fall short of performance on more open-ended tasks, such as designing an AI evaluation—in a preprint from August, he and his collaborators reported that AI models are not yet able to reproduce human computer science research on their own. And in a Wednesday blog post, OpenAI reported that its models don’t do as well on the real-world tasks its employees assign them as they do on the easier, more verifiable tasks in METR’s original suite.

Still, people disagree about how to interpret current performance differences on easily verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks, Kapoor says. Though he thinks that research taste—the ability to choose promising questions, hypotheses, and experiments—will prove a major bottleneck in automating AI R&D, others contend that models trained on easy-to-verify tasks will eventually be able to successfully complete open-ended tasks as well. And progress on verifiable tasks doesn’t seem to be slowing down.

Even if the models do lag behind human performance on open-ended tasks right now, the new report suggests that they might be getting better. Some of the newest models, such as Opus 5.5, tend to achieve what METR calls “borderline above the bar” performance on the evaluation design tasks—not yet usable for METR's research, but promising. Just a year ago, every model was scoring in the “clearly below the bar” category.

But because these open-ended and judgment-heavy tasks are so tough to design and score, METR includes few of them in its report, and that makes it difficult to predict whether and how models might continue to progress in these areas. “The improvement we observe, I think that does tell us something for the current moment,” notes Najoung Kim, a linguist and computer scientist at Boston University. “I’m not sure just yet how to think about how it would extrapolate.”.

Sources indicate that matt Putz, a member of the technical staff at METR, says that predicting progress on these kinds of tasks is likely to remain difficult. “By their nature, hard-to-verify or judgment-laden tasks are much harder to study, and especially to quantify,” he said in an email. “Ultimately, I don’t think we’ll be able to establish trends as clean and robust as for the easy-to-specify [tasks].”.

Recent findings suggest that in general, METR is clearly butting up against the practical difficulties of testing AI performance on difficult and underspecified tasks—precisely the ones most relevant to automating AI R&D. METR’s time horizon plots score task difficulty by evaluating how long it would take a human to complete the task, and for the original plot they measured this quantity by actually having people try each task.

In the latest report, however, the completion times are mostly estimates, because paying people for tasks that might take hundreds of hours, or that only a few experts are qualified to complete, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. Other tasks have more specific shortcomings—for example, for the philosophical argument task, just one person rated most of the arguments, and agents are judged by how well they agree with that particular individual. It’s possible that the scores would change if more experts were surveyed—but that, too, is time-consuming.

It’s still early days for evaluating models on tasks that are hard to validate or require judgment. And while the experts I spoke with see the inclusion of these tasks in METR’s newest time horizon plot as a clear step in the right direction, they agree that we are still far from achieving any definitive answers about whether, and how quickly, automated AI R&D might be coming. “This move toward open-ended tasks is promising,” Kapoor says. But, he adds, “there is just such a lot more to be done to actually get a fuller understanding.”.
