Recent findings suggest that the AWS Quick web app now brings the Quick desktop experience to your browser. Create, share, and use the same agents and skills as on desktop, with the same connectors. Start each day with a daily briefing and a prioritized feed of the email and messages that need your attention. Quick keeps your conversations, agents, and files synchronized across web, desktop, and mobile, so work you start on one surface carries over to the others. Your dashboards, topics, and spaces work as before.

Sources indicate that additionally, agents you start or schedule from the web keep running after you close your browser. Schedule an agent in the morning, answer its questions from the mobile app between meetings, and review the results on your desktop. Recent findings suggest that amazon CloudWatch Omni now supports collecting Azure resource logs, Azure Monitor platform metrics, virtual network (VNet) flow logs, and traces from Application Insights. Teams that run workloads on both AWS and Azure no longer need separate monitoring tools or custom pipelines to see their whole environment. Central operations, DevOps, and site reliability engineering (SRE) teams can now view Azure telemetry alongside their AWS telemetry in one place.

In a recent development, to get started, connect a Microsoft Entra ID tenant to your AWS account and Region. You can choose the telemetry types, subscriptions, Azure regions, resource types, and tags to collect. Azure telemetry lands in Amazon CloudWatch, and Omni spaces can monitor applications and infrastructure across cloud providers. For example, during an incident you can trace a slow request from an Azure-hosted service to its AWS dependencies without switching consoles. You can set up the connectors in the Amazon CloudWatch Omni console or with the AWS CLI.

Azure telemetry collection is available in all Azure Public Regions and can be ingested to all regions where CloudWatch Omni is available. To get started, visit the  CloudWatch Omni User Guide  and for pricing visit pricing page.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The next $1T organization will be a software company masquerading as a services firm.
  • It has been revealed that every founder building an AI tool is asking the same question: what happens when the next version of Claude makes my product a feature?
  • In a recent development, writing code is mostly intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The next $1T organization will be a software company masquerading as a services firm.

It has been revealed that every founder building an AI tool is asking the same question: what happens when the next version of Claude makes my product a feature? Theyâre right to worry. If you sell the tool, youâre in a race against the model. But if you sell the work, every improvement in the model makes your service faster, cheaper, and harder to compete with. A company might spend $10K a year for QuickBooks and $120K on an accountant to close the books. The next legendary company will just close the books.

In a recent development, writing code is mostly intelligence. Knowing what to build next is judgement.

It has been revealed that translating a spec into code, testing, debugging: the rules are complex but they are rules. Judgement is different. It requires experience and taste, instinct built on years of practice. Deciding which feature to build next, whether to take on tech debt, when to ship before itâs ready.

Sources indicate that A year ago, most Cursor users treated AI as autocomplete. Today, more tasks are started by agents than by humans. Software engineering accounts for over half of all AI tool usage across professions. Every other category is still in single digits. The reason is that software engineering is primarily intelligence work. AI has crossed the threshold where it can do most of the intelligence work autonomously and leave the judgement to humans. Software engineering got there first. It is coming to every single profession.

According to recent reports, A copilot sells the tool. An autopilot sells the work.

Until recently, AI models were still developing intelligence and judgement, so the right approach was to build a copilot first: put AI in the hands of a professional and let them decide what to do with it. Harvey sells to law firms. Rogo sells to investment banks. The professional is the customer, the tool makes them more productive, and they take responsibility for the output.

Today, the models are intelligent enough that in some categories the best place to start is as an autopilot. Crosby sells to the tech giant that needs an NDA drafted, not to outside counsel. WithCoverage sells to the CFO who needs insurance, not to the broker. The customer is buying the outcome directly. The work budget in any profession dwarfs the tool budget, and autopilots capture the work budget from day one.

The higher the intelligence ratio in any field, the sooner autopilots will win.

Todayâs judgement will become tomorrowâs intelligence. As AI systems accumulate proprietary data about what good judgement looks like in their domain, the frontier will shift. Copilots and autopilots will converge. The copilot-to-autopilot transition has already begun in several categories. But the starting position matters because it determines where autopilots can win customers now and begin compounding the data that will eventually let them handle judgement too.

The Autopilot Playbook: Outsourcing as the Wedge.

For every dollar spent on software, six are spent on services.

Industry observers note that the total addressable market for autopilots is all labour spend in a category, insourced and outsourced combined. But the right place to start is where outsourcing already exists.

In a recent development, if a task is already outsourced, it tells you three things. One, the tech giant has accepted that this work can be done externally. Two, thereâs an existing budget line that can be substituted cleanly. Three, the buyer is already purchasing an outcome. Replacing an outsourcing contract with an AI-native services provider is a vendor swap. Replacing headcount is a reorg.

It has been revealed that the playbook: companies should start with the outsourced, intelligence-heavy task. Nail distribution. Expand toward the insourced, judgement-heavy work as the AI compounds. The outsourced task is the wedge. The insourced work is the long-term TAM.

Crosby started with NDAs: a well-defined task, primarily intelligence, that most companies already outsource to external counsel. The budget exists, the scope is clear, the ROI is immediate, and the substitution is frictionless.

Industry observers note that plotting every services vertical on an intelligence-to-judgement spectrum and outsourced-to-insourced ratio produces a priority map with labour TAM in brackets. The list is illustrative.

According to recent reports, insurance brokerage ($140-200B). The largest dollar market on this list. Standard commercial lines are highly standardised: the brokerâs value-add is essentially shopping across carriers and filling forms, pure intelligence work. The distribution layer is incredibly fragmented, tens of thousands of small brokers each running the same process, so no single incumbent controls the customer relationship. WithCoverage and Harper are interesting newcomers.

Accounting and audit ($50-80B outsourced in the US alone). The US has lost roughly 340,000 accountants over five years while demand has grown. 75% of CPAs are nearing retirement, the licensing path is long, and starting salaries lag tech and finance. That structural shortage is pushing firms to accept AI faster than almost any other profession. Rillet is building the AI-native ERP that will close the books. Basis started as a copilot for accountants.

Sources indicate that healthcare revenue cycle ($50-80B outsourced in US). People hear âhealthcareâ and assume itâs judgement-heavy, but the billing layer is almost pure intelligence. Medical coding is translating clinical notes into ~70,000 standardised ICD-10 codes. The rules are complex but they are rules. The outsourcing is already mature and outcome-based. An autopilot just has to do the same thing at lower cost. Anterior is the furthest along.

In a recent development, claims adjusting ($50-80B including TPAs). On the other side of the insurance policy, claims adjusting is a separate autopilot surface. Standard-line claims are settled by interpreting policy language against damage schedules and setting reserves using actuarial tables. The adjuster workforce is aging out and nobodyâs replacing them. The market is massively outsourced to independents and TPAs like Crawford and Sedgwick. One industry, at least two distinct autopilot opportunities. Pace is building the autopilot for claims handling. Strala is building an AI-native TPA.

In a recent development, tax advisory ($30-35B). CPA licensing creates a regulatory moat, but 80-90% of the underlying work is intelligence. Every additional jurisdiction a tax autopilot handles deepens its data moat. Multi-jurisdiction complexity is exactly what SMBs outsource because no single in-house accountant can cover it. TaxGPT is an early mover alongside Skalar and Ravical in Europe.

Legal, transactional work ($20-25B). Contract drafting, NDAs, regulatory filings: high intelligence, routinely outsourced. The work product is standardised enough that quality is verifiable, so the buyer can trust AI output without deep legal expertise. Harvey is the emerging leader and is moving quickly to autopilot; Crosby and Lawhive are the autopilot-native newcomers.

IT managed services ($100B+). Every SMB outsources its IT. Patching, monitoring, user provisioning, alert triage: intelligence work running on repeat across thousands of identical environments. The existing software layer (ConnectWise, Datto) sells tools to the MSP. Nobody has yet sold âyour IT runsâ directly to the organization as an outcome. Edra is automating IT processes. Serval is automating IT support.

Recent findings suggest that supply chain and procurement ($200B+). Most enterprises negotiate seriously with only their top 20% of suppliers. The long tail gets zero attention because itâs not economical to have humans do the work. Contract leakage runs 2-5% of total procurement spend. The wedge is abandoned work: no budget line to justify, no incumbent to displace, just found money. Magentic is building the AI for direct procurement, AskLio for indirect procurement. Tacto is building both the system of record and copilot for the midmarket.

Recruitment and staffing ($200B+). The largest services market on this list. The top of the hiring funnel (screening, matching, outreach) is pure intelligence, but closing a candidate and assessing culture fit is judgement built on years of pattern recognition. The autopilot wedge exists in high-volume, low-judgement roles where matching is standardised. Juicebox, Mercor, Jack & Jill are emerging leaders building across the spectrum.

According to recent reports, management consulting ($300-400B). Huge market but the work is mostly judgement. The interesting question is whether AI can disaggregate consulting into intelligence components (data gathering, benchmarking) and judgement components (strategic recommendations), with the intelligence layer getting automated and the judgement layer staying human. Best candidates TBD.

In 2025, the fastest-growing AI companies were copilots. In 2026, many will try to become autopilots. They have the product and the customer knowledge. But they also face the innovatorâs dilemma: selling the work means cutting their own customers out of doing it. Thatâs the opening for pure-play autopilots.

These Plugable cables all feature an E-Marker chip and allow charging up to 240W (48V/5A), but because they don’t have any data lines, all attempts at communication between the charger and the device being charged are blocked.

ChargerLAB Power-Z AK001 display showing voltage, amperage, and power. / Adrian Kingsley-Hughes/ZDNET.

This is five-foot/1.5-meter-long USB-C cable is capable of carrying 240W of power with a built-in USB power meter.

Also: My 7 essential laptop-bag items after decades of working remotely.

It’s totally user-friendly — you just plug it in at both ends, and the display instantly lights up, providing all the crucial statistics about the power flowing through the cable: voltage, amps, and watts.

In a recent development, the display even has an arrow showing the direction that the power is flowing in! This is a great touch because I’ve encountered power meters that have confused me as to what’s charging what — especially where power banks are concerned.

This might be one of the best USB-C accessories I’ve ever purchased. Although simple and straightforward, it has protected my USB-C ports from damage numerous times and prevented laptops from being pulled to the floor by people (usually me) tripping over the charging cable.

Sources indicate that it’s a magnetic breakaway USB-C connector similar to Apple’s MagSafe connector, compatible with all your devices, from smartphones and tablets to power banks, docks, and laptops. The best thing is that it doesn’t slow down data transfer or charging.

Also: 10 cheap car gadgets worth every penny (we’ve tested them all).

The magnetic breakaway USB-C connector consists of two parts: the first part is the USB-C port that plugs into the device you want to protect — be that a laptop, smartphone, charger, power bank, or other device — and the other part goes on the end of the cable you’re going to use.

Sources indicate that super-strong neodymium magnets keep the two parts together when in use until there’s a pull on the connector, and then the two parts come apart. The magnets are very strong and pull the two parts together with a decisive snap. It’s a simple idea yet brilliantly designed.

Got a random cable laying about and need to know what it’s capable of? For this job, the right tool is the Treedix multifunction USB cable tester. This pocket-sized gadget can tell you everything you need to know about a cable (probably more than you need to), and it does it swiftly and reliably.

The USB cable tester is a small box featuring an array of ports. There are USB-C and USB-A output ports and corresponding USB-C, Lightning, miniUSB, and microUSB 2.0 and microUSB 3.0 input ports for testing cables.

Also: Your headphones’ USB-C port has 4 hidden features – but you need the right cable.

The unit can handle a multitude of tests, from basic functions showing whether the cable can handle data and power transmission, along with that protocols, a printout of active lines in the cable, a resistance test, and an eMarker chip test.

If the cable being tested is equipped with an eMarker chip, you will also get information about the maximum current and voltage the cable can carry, the data transfer rate, the type of cable, and even the length of the cable.

Recent findings suggest that awhile back, I was deep in research on the next generation of security infrastructure, talking to CISOs and security engineers at some of the most technically sophisticated companies in Silicon Valley. I asked them all the same question Iâd asked a decade earlier when I worked in enterprise software: Whatâs your biggest headache? The consistency of their answers surprised me. âWe drown in logs we canât afford to keep,â as one security leader put it, âand go blind on the logs we canât afford to search.â.

Enterprise security today is a story of impossible choices. The tools that teams rely on generate enormous amounts of log dataâevery API call, every login event, every network connection. To investigate cyber threats, they need all of it, often going back a year or more. But storing everything in a SIEM like Splunk is prohibitively expensive; costs could easily consume 15% of a CISOâs entire budget. Instead, companies make a compromise: they keep only the most recent 10 to 30 days of logs in their SIEM and park the rest in Amazon S3, where storage is cheap, but the data is effectively frozen. When a breach, a compliance audit, or a forensic investigation happens, security teams discover too late that the evidence they need is out of reach, opaque and unsearchable.

I first heard about Scanner from a member of the security team at Temporal, one of our portfolio companies, who called it, âcrazy fast.â I looked into it, and reached out to Cliff Crosland right away.

Recent findings suggest that what Cliff and his co-founder Steven Wu have built is elegant in its insight. They asked: what would a log search engine look like if you designed it from scratch for object storage? The answer was a purpose-built inverted index that maps field values directly to file regions in S3. Rather than combing through billions of rows, Scanner narrows each query to only the relevant slices of data. A petabyte of logs becomes interactive. Queries that took hours now run in seconds. And a streaming detection engine runs hundreds of detection rules continuously across tens of terabytes a day, without re-scanning the world for each one.

Benchling replaced another product after a forced tenfold price increase, and their head of security engineering called it one of the best technical decisions their team had made. Ramp started with security logs and then expanded to application logs, reducing their SIEM bill in the process. Notionâs detection and response team built an internal AI agent that autonomously runs security investigations using Scanner.

That last example signals whatâs to come. We are entering a new era of security operations, where AI agents will do much of the investigative work that today consumes hours of human time. But agents need to rapidly iterate, ask questions and follow threads; queries canât take minutes, much less hours. Scannerâs speed is enabling these agentic security workflows across a wide range of companies: within weeks of their MCP release, nearly a third of Scannerâs customers were already using it in production, and agents now account for 80% of queries on the platform. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • I've been testing smart bird feeders for more than two years in my own backyard, and Birdfy has been—and still is—the brand I trust and recommend most.
  • Below are the models I've tested—in some cases for years—and recommend, including a couple I personally plan to buy as gifts this year.
  • It has been revealed that WIRED first reviewed this feeder in 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I've been testing smart bird feeders for more than two years in my own backyard, and Birdfy has been—and still is—the brand I trust and recommend most. These feeders are well-made, reliable, and reasonably priced. The brand's app is also excellent; it's easy to navigate and use without shelling out for an additional subscription. Better still, Birdfy just rolled out free lifetime AI ID (which is quite decent) with any bird feeder, including the lowest-priced models. If you don't want to gift a traditional feeder, you might consider Birdfy's smart birdbath and nesting box, each of which comes equipped with the same high-quality camera(s).

Below are the models I've tested—in some cases for years—and recommend, including a couple I personally plan to buy as gifts this year.

It has been revealed that WIRED first reviewed this feeder in 2022. Back then we loved the concept, but felt its AI ID didn't quite cut it. Birdfy has come a long way since then on the AI front. The feeder body is largely the same, but the app and AI ID (now free) are both much improved, offering a seamless and user-friendly experience that makes it easy to sort through which birds visited that day. This once-pricey feeder is now at the lowest price I have ever seen for the version without the solar panel. The 5200-mAh rechargeable battery lasts a few weeks, but I think it's convenient to not have to bring it in to charge, if you want to spring for the extra $20 for that solar panel.

Birdfy's “beginner” model, this unit is basically a gravity pet feeder with a camera on the side. All you need to do is snap three pieces together, charge the camera, and pair it to the Birdfy app. If you know anyone who loves birds but is intimidated by the thought of having to set up and calibrate a smart bird feeder, this could be the perfect gift for them. However, note that my test unit keeps losing its lid on windy days, and there's no roof to keep the seed from getting wet on rainy days, so it's probably best for summer use. I also just discovered that Walmart carries an exclusive periwinkle color that looks lovely.

Industry observers note that birdfy's Metal 2 4K is the brand's flagship release for this year, with Ultra 4K resolution and dual-band (2.4 GHz and 5.0 GHz) Wi-Fi connection. The metal body claims to resist squirrels, and the muted green color is a welcome change from Birdfy's usual bright plastics. As was the case with the brand's previous flagship, the Feeder 2 Pro, I had some significant connection issues with the Metal 2 4K. This kept it from being a top pick in my guide to the Best Smart Bird Feeders, but the model is still worth a mention here due to its combination of features and build quality, as well as Birdfy's excellent customer service if something does go wrong.

Smart bird feeders aren't always the most aesthetically pleasing thing you could put in your yard, but Birdfy's 2K bamboo model was the first smart feeder I've ever had that actually garnered compliments. The natural wood and waterfall-style black roof complement any landscaping or exterior decor, and the camera and overall setup ran flawlessly for me during my months of testing. Just make sure you apply varnish or urethane regularly to the bamboo, as the finish on mine peeled after only two months in mild weather.

Recent findings suggest that this interesting product pairs a plastic birdbath (on an optional metal stand) with a solar-powered camera, so you can keep an eye on visiting birds without having to deal with seed mess. When I first tested it, I was worried birds would splash water on the camera lens, but the most popular activity at the bath is by far drinking the water (birds, raccoons, squirrels … anything passing by). I don't love that the basin grows algae rapidly and the pump clogs easily, but this is otherwise a very well-made item—it's been in my yard for a year and a half through every season, and while the plastic is starting to fade a bit, it's still going strong.

Though I do love a smart bird feeder, Birdfy's Nest Duo is the absolute zenith of bird-watching for me. A black-capped chickadee moved in, laid eggs, and raised chicks (detailed here), and the cameras and app on the Nest stayed working, giving me 24-hour updates with interior night vision and views of the entry hole's exterior to see who was coming and going. A remote control on a 10-foot-long cord lets you reset or charge the camera without bothering the birds (though the auxiliary solar panel worked great for me). Note, however, that the black waterfall-style roof and lack of ventilation do pose a risk of overheating any young birds; during a May heat wave, I had to affix an umbrella and ice packs to the box, but the interior thermometer and hygrometer did a great job keeping me abreast of changing conditions.

These diffusers are also highly convenient to use in that you can control them from your phone via an app (the Home, Plus, and Car also have buttons on the actual devices).

But, it's a luxury you'll pay for. If you own a Pura or have seen it in stores, you already know the scents aren't cheap; single cartridges range from $14 for Pura’s house line all the way up to $21 for name brands like Thymes and Votivo. (The prices displayed on Pura's website look lower, but that's only if you buy a recurring subscription—make sure you note the one-time purchase price.).

Recent findings suggest that cartridges can last for a month or more in the Pura Mini, but in a larger diffuser like the Pura Plus, they may only last a couple of weeks. That's why the best time to stock up on scents for the year is during a sale, like Pura’s Cyber Week event. Right now through December 6, all fragrances are 20 percent off, and all diffusers are 30 percent off.

According to recent reports, pura's diffuser lineup isn't perfect, but neither are any of the diffusers we've tried from any brand. Diffusers can be loud or messy, take up a lot of space, or have an uninspiring line of scents. Pura's Mini and Car models are worthwhile yet quirky (though I can't recommend the Plus), but the Home has given me no challenges in six months of testing.

Sources indicate that if you're in the market for a Pura diffuser, our top pick for most people is the upcoming Pura Home. The first Pura I ever owned was the 3 model, and I've also had the 4, but the 5 (rebranded “Home”) improves on just about everything, with dual-band (2.4 GHz and 5.0 GHz) Wi-Fi compatibility; faster diffusion; control buttons on the device itself; and even a new way to load cartridges, where you can slide out the bottom portion (which is flat to sit on a surface), seat the scents, and click it into place. QR codes on the cartridges inform your app which scents they are and when they were loaded, so it can, in turn, remind you when it's time to replace them. I also like that this model is totally silent.

In a recent development, I also recommend the oval-shaped Mini—I have one in my office right now. Though you can only control it via Pura's app, scents last for over a month, and it does a great job at scenting a smaller space like a bedroom. My unit makes a high-pitched ringing noise, almost like an ultrasonic pest repellent, which is annoying, but Pura's customer service will likely replace yours if this happens to you.

There’s also the Pura Car, whose refills I will be purchasing during this sale (MSRP averages $21 apiece, and the four-week run time has been roughly accurate in my experience). Online reviews of this device are mixed, but I love mine. If you’re a parent, having Pura scents to inhale instead of old, spilled food and stinky soccer cleats is 100 percent worth the spend. Buy one for a mom you know, but only if she has USB charging ports in her car—it needs to be plugged in most of the time, as it doesn’t hold a charge for very long.

Also on sale for 20 percent off is Pura's fun new Advent calendar, which features a Pura Home diffuser and 12 best-selling scents, most of which I have tried and can vouch for being options most people would enjoy.

In a recent development, another Pura Cyber Week deal: Spend $50, and get 50 percent off the Pura Plus diffuser for large spaces, which has an MSRP of $80. I didn’t have the best of luck with the two Plus devices I went through—both eventually developed a loud buzzing noise. (Note that Pura will send you a replacement if this happens to you.) Additionally, unlike the Puras that sit flush to the outlet, this one is a cylinder that sits apart and must be plugged in at all times. It also makes an audible, fixed “shhhhhhh” noise as it’s long as it’s on (unlike the more intermittent noise emitted by competitors). However, it did do a great job of scenting a high-ceilinged room on the first floor of my house.

#22032. Breaking: Don’t Bring Jensen Back

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1326 w)

Breaking: Don’t Bring Jensen Back

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1326 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Early in Shakespeare’s tragedy Julius Caesar, the title character is publicly offered a crown as a symbol of absolute power.
  • Industry observers note that jensen Huang was not so strategic.
  • Sources indicate that huang, used to exercising power, seemed as energized as the mob supporting Caesar had been.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Early in Shakespeare’s tragedy Julius Caesar, the title character is publicly offered a crown as a symbol of absolute power. Caesar refuses it three times, dramatically fainting after the final try. Scholars say that Caesar’s “falling sickness,” as his eventual assassin Brutus put it, masked his true intention to rule. His effort to win over the crowd with his humility only intensified the momentum to grant him more power. Indeed, after his refusal, his adherents became even more impassioned, setting the stage for his eventual claim to kingship. “If Caesar had stabb’d their mothers, they would have done no less,” said a Roman senator of the sycophantic crowd.

Industry observers note that jensen Huang was not so strategic. He did not even wait until a crown was offered before grabbing for it. On November 12, Nvidia’s cofounder had resigned from his post as CEO, promising to work to heal his family and earn back trust. The reasons were obvious. He had been engaging in an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Under his leadership, billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia’s sales had gone to her formerly obscure company in Singapore, which, in a potential violation of export regulations, the company used to power Chinese AI efforts. In addition, he was carrying on an affair with an Nvidia subordinate (or was it two?), itself a fireable transgression. Nonetheless, because of his success in building Nvidia, Huang has been receiving a noisy groundswell of support from Silicon Valley and Wall Street, with the same loyalty as the crowd that would have idolized Caesar even if he’d stabbed their mothers.

Sources indicate that huang, used to exercising power, seemed as energized as the mob supporting Caesar had been. Social media was exploding with memes portraying him as a hero whose return would result in Homeric redemption. Silicon Valley leaders like Travis Kalanick, Tim Sweeney, and Elon Musk called his removal an injustice that must be addressed. One of Huang’s talents is moving fast. So perhaps he used state-of-the-art Rubin GPUs to dispatch an armada of AI introspection-bots, fast-tracking what formerly would have taken months of moral cleansing into a few days. In any case, on November 17, when the pixels on his resignation message had barely settled, he returned to X to announce that he would be honored to reclaim his position if offered.

In a recent development, it was not to be. Within hours, Nvidia’s board threw more water on Huang’s overture than a Texas data center consumes in a year. During a scheduled earnings call, chair Harvey Jones remarked, “The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation but does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO.” Nvidia’s interim leader, Colette Kress, who had been its long-time CFO, ended the call with a devastating kicker: “We’ve got this.” Et tu, Colette?

The search for a replacement will proceed. But even after the board presumably closed the door, and Kress told employees in an all-hands meeting once again that “we got this,” the push to restore him has not quieted. The president of the United States hasn’t retracted his opinion that Huang should resume his post. A petition called “Stand With Jensen” now has over 200,000 signatures. Hedge funder Bill Ackman zinged out a hysterical X post this week charging “major governance failures by directors.” (Clearly, Ackman’s view of ideal governance is no governance.) Most alarmingly, Semafor has reported that Huang himself had spoken to at least one board member about his reinstatement and that several directors may still be open to the possibility. At press time, Huang has not given any public indication that he is no longer angling for a triumphant return.

According to recent reports, at the Upcoming York Times DealBook conference, held a day after the earnings call, the Jensen affair dominated the discussion, even as Anthropic was readying the biggest IPO in history. On stage, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Greg Brockman expressed admiration for Huang but did not recommend his reinstatement. But Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey said that “nobody can take Jensen’s place in this critical juncture” because “his personal relations are the reason everyone is willing to do business” with Nvidia. Elon Musk reaffirmed his outrage that Huang had been forced out, saying it was like the Chicago Bulls firing Michael Jordan in his prime during a playoff hot streak. In my informal conversations during breaks, I found people on both sides of the divide. One person was a substantial Nvidia investor who showed me pictures of themselves with Huang. Like many with a financial stake in the firm, this individual was eager to see Huang back in charge.

In a recent development, everyone is in agreement that the Huang story is tragic. But the outcry for Huang’s reinstatement is a broader tragedy, revealing how greed has eclipsed ethics and patriotism. Those clamoring for reinstatement have one argument: that Huang’s leadership was so singular and superlative that he must keep his job. Not doing so would dishonor his previous efforts and degrade Nvidia’s future performance. Essentially, it’s an ends-justify-the-means rationale incompatible with corporate oversight and even fidelity to law and national security.

In a recent development, the push to reinstate Huang is also a grotesque extension of the cult of the founder, which assumes that those who built a tech giant have unique abilities to run it and should be unconstrained in how they do so. (Serious question: If founders are so great, why do the vast majority of startups fail?).

In a recent development, there’s no question that Huang has built one of the greatest companies ever and delivered historic returns to shareholders. But one irony of the Bring Back Jensen Movement is that this crisis has exposed him, in some respects, as an erratic, even a lousy, CEO. His personal indiscretions cost shareholders almost a trillion dollars! He lied to his board. He pursued a strategy that seems to have violated the spirit if not the law of export regulations. He gave senior executive posts to family members who pursued a passion in the chip business later in life, including his daughter (trained as a chef), son (went to art school and owned a cocktail lounge), and son-in-law (former professional skier). In a public organization, nepotism comes at shareholders’ expense.

On top of that, he failed in a critical duty of a CEO—preparing a succession initiative. Nvidia has none, solely because Huang acted as if he would run it forever. At DealBook, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, after the obligatory expressions of empathy toward Huang, threw some shade on leaders who don’t plan for their departure: “People get old and die,” he remarked. “If a tech giant will succeed, it needs someone to take over. I’ve never trusted a leader, founder or otherwise, who says the institution after I left was completely gone. Like, then what did you build?”.

In a recent development, finally, if Huang were so passionate about Nvidia’s future, why is he still angling for a return? The possibility, even a remote one, that he will be reinstated may discourage the best candidates from considering an offer to lead Nvidia. Huang would best serve Nvidia by shutting down the talk from his Silicon Valley cronies and demanding that the Bring Jensen Back petition be scrapped.

Ultimately, by giving up his quest to reclaim the crown, Huang would better serve not only Nvidia but himself. His energy should be devoted first to mending his family relations and then working with lawyers to maintain his reputation, fortune, and maybe even freedom. There’s an additional bonus to his departure. He will be leaving Nvidia at a peak for high-powered GPU chips and AI’s economic power. If the bubble does pop, Huang will avoid being the face of AI when the fall comes. Remember, things didn’t work out too well for Julius Caesar.

This is an edition of Steven Levy and Lauren Goode’s Backchannel newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

From Hierarchy to Intelligence

📅 31 Mar 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2572 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sequoiacap

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, at Sequoia, we see that speed is the best predictor of start-up success.
  • Two thousand years before the first corporate org chart, the Roman Army solved a problem that every large organization still faces: how do you coordinate thousands of people across vast distances with limited communication?
  • Their answer was a nested hierarchy with a consistent span of control at every level.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, at Sequoia, we see that speed is the best predictor of start-up success. Most companies are focused on AI as a productivity enhancer. Few are focused on the potential of AI to change how we work together. Block is showing what it looks like to fundamentally rethink organization design, ultimately harnessing AI to increase speed as a compounding competitive advantage.

Two thousand years before the first corporate org chart, the Roman Army solved a problem that every large organization still faces: how do you coordinate thousands of people across vast distances with limited communication?

Their answer was a nested hierarchy with a consistent span of control at every level. The smallest unit was the contubernium, eight soldiers who shared a tent, equipment, and a mule, led by a decanus. Ten contubernia formed a century of eighty men under a centurion. Six centuries made a cohort. Ten cohorts made a legion of roughly 5,000. At each layer, a named commander held defined authority, aggregated information from below, and relayed decisions from above. The structure (8 â 80 â 480 â 5,000) was an information routing protocol built around a simple human limitation: a leader can effectively manage somewhere between three and eight people. The Romans discovered this through centuries of warfare. Even today, the US Armyâs hierarchical chain follows a similar pattern. We now call it âspan of control,â and it remains the governing constraint of every large organization on earth.

The next major change came from Prussia. After Napoleonâs army destroyed the Prussian forces at the Battle of Jena in 1806, a group of reformers led by Scharnhorst and Gneisenau rebuilt the military around an uncomfortable truth: you cannot depend on individual genius at the top. You need a system. They created the General Staff, a dedicated class of trained officers whose job was not to fight but to blueprint operations, process information, and coordinate across units. Scharnhorst intended these staff officers to âsupport incompetent Generals, providing the talents that might otherwise be wanting among leaders and commanders.â This was middle management before the term existed. Professionals whose purpose was to route information, pre-compute decisions, and maintain alignment across a complex organization. The military also formalized the distinction between âlineâ and âstaffâ functions. Line advances the core mission. Staff provides specialized support. Every corporation still uses this vocabulary today.

Military hierarchy entered the business world through the American railroads in the 1840s and 1850s. The U.S. Army lent West Point-trained engineers to private railroad companies, and these officers brought military organizational thinking with them. Staff and line hierarchies, divisional structure, bureaucratic systems of reporting and control: all of it was developed in the military before the railroads adopted it. In the mid-1850s, Daniel McCallum of the Upcoming York and Erie Railroad created the worldâs first organizational chart to manage a system stretching over 500 miles with thousands of workers. The informal management styles that worked for smaller railroads were failing. Train collisions were killing people. McCallumâs chart formalized the same hierarchical logic the Romans had used: layers of authority, defined reporting lines, structured information flow. It became the blueprint for the modern corporation.

According to recent reports, frederick Taylor (1856-1915), often called the âFather of Scientific Management,â optimized what happened within that hierarchy. Taylor broke work into specialized tasks, assigned them to trained experts, and managed through measurement rather than intuition. This produced the functional pyramid organization â a structure optimized for efficiency within the information routing system that the military had pioneered and the railroads had commercialized.

The first real stress test of functional hierarchy came during World War II. The Manhattan Project required physicists, chemists, engineers, metallurgists, and military officers to work across disciplinary boundaries toward a single objective under extreme secrecy and time pressure. Robert Oppenheimer organized Los Alamos into functional divisions but insisted on open collaboration across them, resisting the militaryâs instinct to compartmentalize. When the implosion problem became critical in 1944, he reorganized the lab around it, creating cross-functional teams unlike anything in corporate America at the time. It worked, but it was a wartime exception led by a singular figure. The question the postwar business world faced was whether that kind of cross-functional coordination could be made routine.

According to recent reports, with the growth and globalization of companies after World War II, the scale limitations of functional design became acute. In 1959, McKinseyâs Gilbert Clee and Alfred di Scipio published âCreating a World Enterpriseâ in the Harvard Business Review, providing an intellectual framework for a matrix organization that combined functional specialties with divisional units. Under the leadership of Marvin Bower, McKinsey helped companies like Shell and GE implement these principles, balancing central standards with local agility. This became the âprofessionalâ or âmodernâ corporation that propelled the postwar global economy.

Over time, other frameworks emerged to address the complexity, rigidity, and bureaucracy of matrix structures. The McKinsey 7-S framework, developed in the late 1970s by Tom Peters and Robert Waterman, distinguished the âhard Ssâ (Strategy, Structure, Systems) from the âsoft Ssâ (Shared Values, Skills, Staff, Style). The core idea was that structural elements alone were insufficient. Organizational effectiveness required alignment across cultural traits and the human factors that determine whether a strategy actually succeeds.

Recent findings suggest that in more recent decades, technology companies have experimented aggressively with organization structure. Spotify popularized cross-functional squads with short sprint cycles. Zappos attempted Holacracy, eliminating management titles entirely. Valve operated with a flat structure and no formal hierarchy. Each of these experiments revealed something about the limitations of traditional hierarchy, but none solved the underlying problem. Spotify moved back toward conventional management as it scaled. Zappos saw significant attrition. Valveâs model proved difficult to scale beyond a few hundred people. As organizations grow into the thousands, they revert to hierarchical coordination because no alternative information routing mechanism has been powerful enough to replace it.

In a recent development, the constraint is the same one the Romans faced and the Marine Corps rediscovered in World War II: narrowing span of control means adding layers of command, but more layers mean slower information flow. Two thousand years of organizational innovation has been an attempt to work around this tradeoff without breaking it.

At Block, weâre questioning the underlying assumption: that organizations have to be hierarchically organized with humans as the coordination mechanism. Instead, we intend to replace what the hierarchy does. Most companies using AI today are giving everyone a copilot, which makes the existing structure work slightly better without changing it. Weâre after something different: a manufacturer built as an intelligence (or mini-AGI).

We are not the first to try to move beyond traditional hierarchy. Haierâs rendanheyi model, platform organizations, âdata-drivenâ management: these are real attempts at the same problem. What they lacked was a technology capable of actually performing the coordination functions that hierarchy exists to provide. AI is that technology. For the first time, a system can maintain a continuously updated model of an entire business and use it to coordinate work in ways that previously required humans relaying information through layers of management.

For this to work, a company needs two things: a kind of âworld modelâ of its own operations, and a customer signal rich enough to make that model useful.

Recent findings suggest that block is remote-first. Everything we do creates artifacts. Decisions, discussions, code, designs, aims, problems, and progress all exist as recorded actions. Itâs the raw material for a company world model. In a traditional company, a managerâs job is to know whatâs happening across their team and relay that context up and down the chain. In a remote-first company where work is already machine-readable, AI can build and maintain that picture continuously. Whatâs being built, whatâs blocked, where resources are allocated, whatâs working and what isnât. Thatâs the information the hierarchy used to carry. The company world model carries it instead.

Sources indicate that but the capability of the system is only as good as the quality of the customer signal feeding it. And money is the most honest signal in the world.

People lie on surveys. They ignore ads. They abandon carts. But when they spend, save, send, borrow, or repay, thatâs the truth. Every transaction is a fact about someoneâs life. Block sees both sides of millions of these transactions every day, the buyer through Cash App and the seller through Square, plus the operational data from running the merchantâs business. That gives the customer world model something rare: a per-customer, per-merchant understanding of financial reality built from honest signal that compounds. The richer the signal, the better the model. The better the model, the more transactions. The more transactions, the richer the signal.

Together, the company world model and the customer world model form the foundation for a different kind of company. Instead of product teams building predetermined roadmaps, you build four things.

First, capabilities. The atomic financial primitives: payments, lending, card issuance, banking, buy-now-pay-later, payroll, and so on. These are not products. They are building blocks that are hard to acquire and maintain (some have network effects and regulatory permission). They have no UIs of their own. They have reliability, compliance, and performance targets.

Second, a world model. This has two sides. The organization world model is how the company understands itself and its own operations, performance, and priorities, replacing the information that used to flow through layers of management. The customer world model is the per-customer, per-merchant, per-market representation built from proprietary transaction data. It starts with raw transaction data today and evolves toward full causal and predictive models over time.

It has been revealed that third, an intelligence layer. This is what composes capabilities into solutions for specific customers at specific moments and delivers them proactively. A restaurantâs cash flow is tightening ahead of a seasonal dip the model has seen before. The intelligence layer composes a short-term loan from the lending capability, adjusts the repayment schedule using the payments capability, and surfaces it to the merchant before they even think to look for financing. A Cash App userâs spending pattern shifts in a way the model associates with a move to a latest city. The intelligence layer composes a new direct deposit setup, a Cash App Card with boosted categories for their new neighborhood, and a savings goal calibrated to their updated income. No product manager decided to build either solution. The capabilities existed. The intelligence layer recognized the moment and composed them.

It has been revealed that fourth, interfaces (hardware and software). Square, Cash App, Afterpay, TIDAL, bitkey, proto. These are delivery surfaces through which the intelligence layer delivers composed solutions. They are crucial, but they are not where the value is created. The value is in the model and the intelligence.

Sources indicate that when the intelligence layer tries to compose a solution and canât because the capability doesnât exist, that failure signal is the future roadmap. The traditional roadmap, where product managers hypothesize about what to build next, is any companyâs ultimate limiting factor. In this model, customer reality generates the backlog directly.

If this is what the firm builds, then the question becomes: what do the people do?

The org structure follows from this, and it inverts the traditional picture. In a conventional company, the intelligence is spread throughout the people and the hierarchy routes it. In this model, the intelligence lives in the system. The people are on the edge. The edge is where the action is.

Sources indicate that the edge is where the intelligence makes contact with reality. People reach into places the model canât go yet. They sense things the model canât perceive: intuition, opinionated direction, cultural context, trust dynamics, the feeling in a room. They make the calls the model shouldnât make on its own, especially ethical decisions, novel situations, and high-stakes moments where the cost of being wrong is existential. A world model that canât touch the world is just a database. But the edge doesnât need layers of management to coordinate it. The world model gives every person at the edge the context they need to act without waiting for information to travel up and down a chain of command.

In practice, this means we normalize down to three roles.

It has been revealed that individual contributors (ICs) who build and operate capabilities, the model, the intelligence layer, and the interfaces. They are deep specialists and experts in a specific layer of the system. The world model provides the context that a manager used to provide, so ICs can make decisions about their layer without waiting to be told what to do.

In a recent development, directly Responsible Individuals (DRI) who own specific cross-cutting problems or opportunities and customer outcomes. A DRI might own the problem of merchant churn in a specific segment for 90 days, with full authority to pull resources from the world model team, the lending capability team, and the interface team as needed. DRIs may persist on certain problems or move elsewhere to solve new ones.

Player-coaches who combine building with developing people. They replace the traditional manager whose primary job was information routing. A player-coach still writes code or builds models or designs interfaces. They also invest in the growth of the people around them. They donât spend their days in status meetings, alignment sessions, and priority negotiations. The world model handles alignment. The DRI structure handles strategy and priority. The player-coach handles craft and people.

There is no need for a permanent middle management layer. Everything else the old hierarchy did, the system coordinates, and everyone is empowered, with a role thatâs much closer to the work and the customer.

Block is in the early stages of this transition. It will be a difficult one, and parts of it will likely break before they work. Weâre writing about it now because we believe every firm will eventually need to confront the same question we did: what does your company understand that is genuinely hard to understand, and is that understanding getting deeper every day?

If the answer is nothing, AI is just a cost optimization story. You cut headcount, improve margins for a few quarters, and eventually get absorbed by something smarter. If the answer is deep, AI doesnât augment your manufacturer. It reveals what your company actually is.

It has been revealed that blockâs answer is the economic graph: millions of merchants and consumers, both sides of every transaction, financial behavior observed in real time. That understanding compounds every second the system operates. We believe the pattern behind this, a company organized as an intelligence rather than a hierarchy, is significant enough that it will reshape how companies of all kinds operate over the coming years. Block is far enough along to show the idea is more than theory (though, we welcome debate and feedback to pressure test and improve our ideas).

Recent findings suggest that companies move fast or slow based on information flow. Hierarchy and middle management impede information flow. For two thousand years, from the Roman contubernium to todayâs global enterprises, we have had no real alternative. Eight soldiers sharing a tent needed a decanus. Eighty men needed a centurion. Five thousand needed a legate. The question was never whether you needed layers. The question was whether humans were the only option for what those layers do. They arenât anymore. Block is building what comes next.

Internet Archive Staffers Are Unionizing

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (619 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Staffers at the Internet Archive, the nonprofit “digital library” that runs the Wayback Machine, are voting to join the Communications Workers of America (CWA).
  • More than 80 of the 124 eligible US staffers voted in favor of unionizing, and they are presently awaiting voluntary recognition of the union from Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle.
  • The Internet Archive, which also offers free catalogs preserving tens of millions of digital and physical media items, was founded by Kahle in 1996.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Staffers at the Internet Archive, the nonprofit “digital library” that runs the Wayback Machine, are voting to join the Communications Workers of America (CWA).

More than 80 of the 124 eligible US staffers voted in favor of unionizing, and they are presently awaiting voluntary recognition of the union from Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle. Kahle did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment. If Kahle does not grant voluntary recognition, employees will vote whether to certify the union in a process run by the National Labor Relations Board.

The Internet Archive, which also offers free catalogs preserving tens of millions of digital and physical media items, was founded by Kahle in 1996. Kahle’s mission was to provide “Universal Access to All Knowledge.” Will Howes, an Internet Archive engineer, says that the organizing process has demonstrated how “aligned” employees are in their passion for Kahle’s goals.

“Frankly, we really see the formation of this union as accepting [Kahle’s] challenge to make this workplace the best place it can be in pursuit of a mission, universal access to all knowledge,” Howes tells WIRED.

Microfiche digitization technician Danielle Leard tells WIRED that the union is “very optimistic” that Kahle will voluntarily recognize it and come to the bargaining table. They add that among the union’s core goals are securing wage increases and additional benefits, and ensuring that these benefits are consistently available to employees across the manufacturer.

“We believe the first and most primary goal of our union is to make sure that the Internet Archive reflects the wants and values of the people that work there, and the people that make the archive,” Leard says.

It has been revealed that howes and Leard tell WIRED that the Internet Archive—which claims to have archived more than 1 trillion web pages—employs a highly diverse set of workers, including librarians, engineers, physical media specialists, and facility coordinators who maintain the archive’s building, a former Christian Scientist church in San Francisco. Leard says that the staff’s diversity has made the organizing process, which began in February 2025, “a unique challenge,” but one that’s “really rewarding.”.

According to recent reports, the vote comes slightly more than two months after staffers at the Wikimedia Foundation, the nonprofit behind Wikipedia, voted to join CWA. Howes indicates the simultaneous efforts are “very powerful” given that both organizations represent “core infrastructure” of the internet.

Howes states that the union wants to ensure that the 30-year-old project continues to thrive in the long term—and that its workers do too. Leard says this means providing paths for developing skills and getting promoted within the nonprofit.

Leard indicates that the Internet Archive’s unionization drive is especially important in the present moment, amid waves of tech layoffs and widespread anxiety about “emerging technologies” like AI.

The Internet Archive hasn’t been immune from the consequences of AI. A Nieman Lab report from January found that some news websites, struggling to prevent companies like OpenAI or Anthropic from harvesting their articles, have started blocking web crawlers from the Internet Archive, arguing it gives AI companies a back door to their content. (The archive relies on web crawlers to preserve news articles in near-real time.).

Leard notes that ideally, the Internet Archive’s unionization will be “one domino” in a larger process that makes the tech industry better.

“We're hoping,” they say, “that we'll continue to be one of the blueprints that will make it easier for other organizations and companies in the future to continue to unionize.”.

Upgrade: 11/20/26 1:43pm ET: This story has been updated to reflect that Internet Archive workers have voted in favor of unionizing, but the union has not yet been recognized by Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jensen Huang was ousted from Nvidia amid allegations of extramarital affairs, including a relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.
  • In a recent development, while Huang admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang on November 8, the board couldn’t determine in the moment whether she was an intelligence operative for China, these sources say.
  • But in the following days, once allegations of other affairs surfaced, including one reportedly with a direct report, “what could be determined was [Huang’s] lying, and that spanned a year, from October 2025 through recent events,” a source close to the board told WIRED, who requested anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak on its behalf.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jensen Huang was ousted from Nvidia amid allegations of extramarital affairs, including a relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. Yet it was “multiple challenges” related to Huang’s “lack of candor” and “lying” that ultimately moved the board of directors, according to two people familiar with private discussions among the chair and other members.

In a recent development, while Huang admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang on November 8, the board couldn’t determine in the moment whether she was an intelligence operative for China, these sources say. That same day, the board announced an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting” that their CEO had “been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has rejected allegations that Alice Huang was a spy.

But in the following days, once allegations of other affairs surfaced, including one reportedly with a direct report, “what could be determined was [Huang’s] lying, and that spanned a year, from October 2025 through recent events,” a source close to the board told WIRED, who requested anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak on its behalf.

In a recent development, according to sources, members of the board had asked Huang about Alice Huang after The New York Times first reported in October 2025 that Nvidia had an unusually robust business relationship with a Singapore-based data center manufacturer named Megaspeed, where Alice Huang had worked. Jensen Huang at the time denied any inappropriate relationship with Alice Huang to the board, sources tell WIRED.

After the affair came to light, the board was incensed, these people say. A source familiar with the board’s thinking told WIRED that while these board members view issues of national security as “key” and “ongoing,” the primary driver behind Huang’s ouster was “the lying.”.

“It was a matter of integrity and trust,” this person remarked.

Industry observers note that in recent days, board members, including chair Harvey Jones, have tried to quell the discourse about Huang’s possible return to Nvidia by emphasizing that Huang's behavior flew in the face of Nvidia’s policies and corporate governance rules, sources tell WIRED. While previous reporting by WIRED and other news outlets have outlined factors that Jones has remarked played into the board’s decision, the primary motivation hadn’t been previously specified.

Sources indicate that board chair Harvey Jones did not respond to a WIRED request for comment. A spokesperson for Nvidia, John Rizzo, declined to comment. John Fisher, vice president at the communications firm Trident, which is representing Huang, declined to comment except to say that Huang voluntarily resigned from his positions at Nvidia.

In a recent development, for Nvidia’s board, the possibility that Alice Huang was working on behalf of the Chinese government poses a bigger problem than an executive’s personal misconduct. If she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, the scandal isn’t just about Huang’s alleged “lack of candor,” but a potential security and governance crisis.

In a recent development, already, the scandal has given China hawks grist to call for tighter controls on US business dealings with China. In addition, multiple government agencies and offices have called for investigations into what the former Nvidia CEO may have known about the manufacturer’s chips getting into China. The company’s general counsel, Tim Teter, has also been called to Washington, DC, to testify, as government officials try to find out more about Nvidia’s possible flouting of export controls.

Nvidia and Huang are also facing several shareholder lawsuits, alleging the CEO and the company made misleading statements about dealings with Alice Huang and Megaspeed. Other Silicon Valley investors have publicly raised concerns about insufficient corporate governance and executive oversight by the board.

In the company’s all-hands meeting on November 18, board chair Jones remarked it was “not an easy decision to accept [Huang’s] resignation,” according to remarks reviewed by WIRED. “However, the disclosure of personal behavior and a lack of candor inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards, and values made this a necessary decision.”.

Meanwhile, fans and supporters of Huang, including thousands of Nvidia employees and Elon Musk, have continued to call for his return to Nvidia. Huang himself has mentioned he would be “honored” to come back as CEO. Industry observers note that the news outlet Semafor reported that a small faction of Nvidia’s board of directors has pushed to bring Huang back as well. Jones has not responded to WIRED’s inquiries about the board’s reported division on the topic of Huang’s return.

Some employees are miffed at how quickly the board accepted Huang’s resignation, insisting the longtime leader must have been the victim of a coordinated campaign intended to unseat him. “We feel like they forced his hands to resign,” claims one person on the business side at Nvidia. “We don’t understand why the board is so adamant about not giving him a second chance.”.

At the all-hands meeting, interim CEO Colette Kress said employees’ biggest concern was Nvidia’s falling share price. The next biggest concern was the board’s decision to oust Huang. But while she addressed the first by moving up pay raises, she offered no promise on sharing results of the board’s investigation into Huang or its deliberations about him.

“The ship has sinked but there’s no plan to be transparent about what happened,” notes one computer scientist working at Nvidia. “It feels like a black box.”.

What does it mean to build a mind that is not a copy of our own?

Today, we are excited to announce that Sequoia is partnering with David Silver and Ineffable Intelligence, a newly introduced AI research lab based in London with a singular mission: to make first contact with superintelligence.

Sources indicate that ineffable is building what David calls a superlearner: a system that discovers all knowledge directly through its own experience, from elementary motor skills to profound intellectual breakthroughs. No pre-training. No imitation. Just an agent learning endlessly from the consequences of its own actions in a world built to teach it.

Industry observers note that A Reinforcement Learning-based superlearner has the potential to rediscover and then transcend the greatest inventions in human history: language, science, mathematics and technology. Imagine a machine that derives the laws of physics from first principles. That invents newly introduced branches of mathematics we never thought to ask about. That designs materials, medicines and computers we donât yet have the vocabulary to describe. This is the prize David is reaching for.

Industry observers note that the current generation of AI was built by training on the entirety of the human internet. It is an extraordinary achievement. But a system trained on human data may also have fundamental limitations.

According to recent reports, ineffable Intelligence is scaling reinforcement learning from a clean base: no pre-training, no human data to shortcut the system. Guided by the Era of Experience as a north star, David is proving that agents trained purely from an environment can develop non-human strategies for reasoning about problems we donât yet know how to solve.

In a recent development, david led some of the defining breakthroughs in deep reinforcement learning, most famously in the devilishly difficult game of Go. Go is the ultimate machine intelligence test because it cannot be brute-forced by a computer: a combinatorially explosive O(10^170) possible legal board positions vastly exceeds the O(10^80) atoms in the observable universe. It was thought to be simply too hard for machines to solve.

Sources indicate that at DeepMind, David drove the key breakthrough that finally solved the game of Go: self-play. Self-play drove the ~800 ELO-point leap that led to the historic AlphaGo vs. Lee Sedol showdown in March 2016. David pushed the idea further still with AlphaGo Zero: removing human pre-training entirely and learning purely through self-play increased the systemâs ELO rating from ~3,700 to 5,000+. The result was a system that reached decisively superhuman performance, and with somewhat non-human mannerisms.

Thatâs the lineage David has spent his career building. He was the lead researcher and technical force behind the Alpha series at DeepMind, where, for a brilliant period, his approach was the dominant paradigm: AlphaGo, AlphaZero, AlphaStar, AlphaProof and more.

Even with the arrival of LLMs, David never stopped believing. He is one of the very few people on earth with the conviction, the technical depth and the team to scale reinforcement learning.

The work ahead is hard, the timeline to superintelligence is uncertain, and the bet is genuinely contrarian. That is exactly what excites us. The largest leaps in AI have always come from people willing to ignore the consensus. David has ignored more consensus, more correctly, than almost anyone in the field.

We are honored to co-lead Ineffableâs first round and to partner with David on what may be the most ambitious scientific mission of our generation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Listening to the in-game radio stations while you cruise around in Grand Theft Auto VI, you might hear a recruitment ad for the Vice City Police Department, which makes no secret of the kind of maladjusted psychos it's looking for.

Recent findings suggest that “Have you always dreamed of abusing your power without consequence?” one spot begins. “Well, now you can, when you join the Vice City Police Department, VCPD. You’ll have fun learning the ins and outs of applying excessive force.” The commercial goes on to suggest that cadets will be trained in racial profiling and planting evidence.

Recent findings suggest that given that blistering analysis of American law enforcement, you might imagine that actual cops aren’t big fans of the latest GTA title, which was released after a 13-year wait on Thursday. Yet as millions of gamers have started to explore every stash house and back alley in the sun-drenched wilderness of a fictionalized South Florida, even police departments have attempted to exploit this monocultural mania to elevate their public messaging or recruit new officers.

It’s a curious strategy given that the series rewards theft and drug dealing while enticing you to run over pedestrians, but evidently the mere presence of law enforcement in the games (as the primary antagonists, mind you) was enough to inspire waves of AI slop celebrating the thin blue line.

An Instagram channel of the San Diego Police Department, for example, on Thursday posted an AI-generated image of an SDPD cruiser set against a sunset over the San Diego Bay. Its neon pinks and purples match the saturated aesthetic of GTA, and in case there was any doubt what the department was going for, the nonsensical phrase “Join San Diego PD VI” appears at the top. “Want to drive a police car, we can make that happen!” reads the caption. “Apply Now!”.

Sources indicate that another police department in Washington state shared GTA-like imagery on its Instagram page, encouraging viewers to try “the real-life version” of GTA VI by pursuing a career in law enforcement. “No cheat codes,” the caption advertised. “No respawns. Just real people, real challenges, and a career that makes a difference.” A wave of self-serious GTA slop also flooded the feeds of police departments in Canada, from Edmonton to Toronto—though the Calgary Police Service tried something more lighthearted by having one of their traffic officers react to clips of dangerous and illegal driving maneuvers in the game.

In a recent development, among police departments that were not seeking to add to their ranks through GTA VI fever, many posted content aimed at reminding people that laws exist in real life. “Keep It In The Game VI,” advised a typical post on the Instagram account of the Glendale Police Department in California, complete with a GTA-fied police cruiser and view of the city. “Follow posted speed limits, respect the law, and keep your wanted level at ZERO!” the caption warned. The Denver Police Department, in similarly scolding fashion, informed followers: “Grand theft auto is still illegal.”.

The communications teams for these agencies should have perhaps reconsidered trying to farm engagement and clout from the massive success of GTA VI. As many commenters are noting, the game portrays cops as corrupt and quick to violence. Players have discovered that the Vice City squad will brutalize you if you start filming them during a questionable arrest. One clip highlighted a cop pulling his weapon on a character who had done nothing worse than stand in the street to take a selfie.

A certain dose of this authoritarian cruelty ought to appeal to the right-wing cranks upset that GTA VI is too “woke” when it comes to gender, race, and politics overall. It’s a little different when the most visible villains of the game are choosing to overlook its vicious take on their profession in order to spam epic social media posts.

Fox News, just for comparison, dutifully took the tired law-and-order line on GTA VI, with talking heads aghast at kids’ exposure to virtual gun violence (never mind actual gun deaths in the US) and an atmosphere of moral depravity. Elon Musk famously declared that he couldn’t play GTA games because they compelled you to shoot cops.

Both stances, however insincere, suggest a modicum of regard for law enforcement that the police departments themselves immediately jettisoned in favor of GTA cringe. They of course won’t win any cool points for it, but at least this way they can pretend to connect with the general population.

In a recent development, more baffling still is that the Russian army has generated its own GTA VI recruitment ads to blast out on its Telegram channel, and NATO has trumpeted its defensive security alliance with military-industrial GTA sludge, boasting that “even the best gamers would have a challenge” eluding fighter jets and submarines. Trying to parse Vice President JD Vance’s depiction of a Trumpian “golden age” with GTA graphics is a fool’s errand. In the most dystopian development of all, a US Army battalion in Georgia granted 43 eligible soldiers four days off to play the new GTA in return for reenlisting for another two years of service.

It has been revealed that what do any of these institutions or their missions have to do with a video game where you rob convenience stores in flip-flops? Doesn’t matter. When the zeitgeist is this all-consuming, you fire up ChatGPT and find an angle, no matter how confusing. Surely someone, somewhere, will be tricked into thinking you have anything to do with it.

The future of useful agents may begin not with text, but with pixels.

The future of useful agents may begin not with text, but with pixels.

Could pixels hold the keys to training useful agents?

The race to scale language models â and the agent ecosystem around them â is white-hot. Coding agents, which reason through problems and write code to solve them, have already taken us very far.

But one ambitious young team is making a different bet: that the most promising path to general computer agents may not run through language, screenshots, and tool calls, but through scaling raw video.

Standard Intelligenceâs thesis is that the best way to build a general agent is through full video pre-training on computer use, because it is the only approach that can truly scale action data. Instead of predicting text tokens, the model learns to use a computer from raw screen data, predicting the next mouse movement, click, and keystroke from the pixels in front of it.

It is the Tesla FSD approach applied to knowledge work on computer screens.

That makes the bet both deeply contrarian and deeply âbitter lessonâ-pilled. Rather than hand-engineering workflows or wrapping language models in increasingly elaborate harnesses, Standard Intelligence is betting on a newly introduced pre-training paradigm: feed the model the raw stream of computer use, scale it aggressively, and let the generality emerge from the data.

It has been revealed that video is unwieldy. It is computationally expensive, economically expensive, and technically unforgiving. Prior attempts to scale video toward AGI have often died on the vine.

Recent findings suggest that the Standard Intelligence team is emphatically ânot video people.â They did not arrive with a decade of inherited assumptions about how to work with video as a medium. Instead, they have had to reason through each challenge from first principles, and have met those challenges with unusual optimism, creativity, and scrappiness.

In a recent development, the results are striking. An 11-million-hour computer action dataset â the largest in the industry. A video encoder that is roughly 50Ã more token-efficient than competing approaches, enabling nearly two hours of 30 FPS video to fit inside a 1-million-token context window. A 30-petabyte storage cluster racked in San Francisco for under $500K, roughly 20Ã cheaper than hyperscaler alternatives.

In a recent development, FDM-1, their first foundation model trained directly on computer-use video at scale, offers an early glimpse of what this paradigm could become. It is a general model that can extrude a CAD gear in Blender, drive a car around a San Francisco block after an hour of fine-tuning, and find bugs in software by exploring its state space the way a curious human might.

Founders Galen Mead and Devansh Pandey met as teenagers during the Atlas Fellowship in 2022, a selective fellowship for high-school students interested in AI alignment and AGI.

It has been revealed that galen and Devansh are unusually serious about reaching AGI, and unusually conscientious about doing so safely. Both founders are wise beyond their years (21 and 20 respectively), and both left their undergraduate programs out of a sense of urgency to work on this problem.

In a recent development, galen and Devansh stand out for their combination of taste, scrappiness, technical courage, and ambition. It shows up in the product thinking, in the research direction, and in the FDM-1 report itself.

According to recent reports, the full team of six is small but mighty. Neel, Yudhister, Ulisse, and Ryan are each quirky and exceptional. They have chosen to turn down the conventional path (fancy degrees and offers from big token) and pursue this courageous mission together.

Video has long been a powerful training ground for AI. DQN indicated that agents could learn rich behavior directly from pixels in Atari environments. Tesla scaled video models to make self-driving cars and robots navigate the physical world.

But in the race toward general knowledge agents, video-first pre-training remains an unconventional idea.

Standard Intelligence is betting that it will not stay unconventional for long.

We are thrilled to lead Standard Intelligenceâs Series A alongside Miko and Yasmin from Spark Capital.

One mechanism has been consistently strong as a full-spectrum signal processor rather than a narrow-band signal amplifier: the market. What comes out the other end is a price: a continuously updated consensus of everyone with money and conviction on the line, stripped of the performance that dominates everywhere else. What if I told you Brooks Running started out making ballet slippers and bathing shoes? Founded in 1914, the Seattle-based company spent decades making just about everything except running shoes, moving from baseball cleats to roller skates, football cleats, children’s shoes, and softball cleats. It wasn’t until 1972 that Brooks made running its focus, and the company has been refining the category ever since.

Brooks introduced one of the industry’s earliest uses of EVA foam, developed the first running shoe with a breathable GORE-TEX upper, and introduced the Kinetic Wedge, an innovative design tailored to women’s anatomy.
